The Wild Birds Protection (County of Cheater) Order, 11191, Dated 15th February, 1898. In rursuance of the powers conferred upon me by the Wild Birds Protection Acts, 1830 to 1896, and upon ap- plication by the County Council of Chester, I hereby make the following Order,which shall apply to the whole of the County of Chester a. way trains. The use of the weed has developed enormously among women of late, and perhaps there is not a single women's clab in the West End that has not set aside a quiet sanctum for those members who use tobacco. I notice that a tea shop in one of the most fashionable streets has just pro- vided a ladies' coffeeroom and smoking-room, into which the sex can steal when fatigued with shop- ping. Rivals will follow the example of this pioneer refreshment house, but why should the advanced women creep into secret corners to enjoy their equality with the domineering male? Would they not sooner gain their victory by defying public opinion, putting the biggest pipe in their mouth they could find, crowding out into the thickest thoroughfares of our grbat towns, and thus outliving ridicule ?

There is an epidemic of measles in the West End of London. Barnum and Bailey's great show has been selected by the West End public as the cause of the outbreak. With such a promiscuous collec- tion of human monstrosities and oddities of all kinds, imaginative people thought themselves justified in fixing upon it as the " fons et origo mali." The managers,however, fee a medical gentle- man to keep a permanent watch over the health of the establishment, and in the present instance he happens to be the medical officer of the parish. The number of the employes exceeds a thousand,and he certifies that there is not a single case of infectious disease among them, and that since the arrival of the show the standard of health has been excep- tionally high. This will reassure the public in those provincial towns which ah so soon to be favoured with a visit from this colossal exhibition.

div.head: EARNINGS OF LADY MUSIC HALL ARTISTES.
div.p: THE EARNINGS OF LADY MUSIC HALL ARTISTES.

The Music Hall and Variety Artistes' Protection Asso- ciation is contesting the right of an agent to draw com- mission when an artiste is unable to fulfil engagements by reason of illhealth. The case in point is not without Interest. A well known serio comic, drawing between £BO and £lOO a week, recently became so indisposed that she was unable to give her full "show,, an the management deducted a portion of her salary. Her agent, however, claimed commission upon the full salary,and this is the point to be fought. That the health of a professional is a matter of the utmost importance is beyond all question,as the public naturally feel disappointed when they learn that a favourite artiste is "indisposed." The story told by one of London's most promising lady artistes, Miss Daisy James, to a "Weekly Dispatch" representative cannot be without interest to her many admirers, and to the public generally. Miss James,who In private life is Mrs. Harry Villiers, wal formerly one of the Sisters Fortesque, but hard work under trying conditions told upon her, and considerable suffering and pecuniary loss resulted. It was not an easy matter to get this quiet, lady-like little artiste to tell the story,but yielding to persuasion she allowed herself to be hater- viewed . I " One who has been before the public professionally ifor some years is apt to be thought older than she really ' Is. I shall not be twenty until next May. A SHARP LITTLE GIRL. —A poorly-clad little village girl went into a stationer's shop. She wished to buy some writing paper, and finally was shown some at 15 cents, a quire. "How much will half a quire be?" she inquired, in a plaintive little voice. "Ten cents.," replied the assistant. "uf you please, I'll take the other half."

- "Yes," said Mr. Smitherkins, as he leaned back from the dessert at the dinner table, "they do say that a woman's work is never done." "And that is just where they're right," said Mrs. S. promptly, "and I am glad to see that you are beginning to realise what a time I have. What made you think of it?" "That pie," returned Suiitherkins, quietly. A UTILITARIAN VIEW.—Some boys made a tar- <Yet of a bottle by setting it. up on a pole. The peripatetic philosopher watched for some tirse their futile efforts to stone it off. Then, feeling that some advice was needed, he said: "Boys, boys, why do you thus waste your time? If you really don't want that bottle there, why don't one of you take a stick and knock it off?" COULDN'T FOOL HER.—" Let me see fiOffle of your black kid gloves," said an agressive-looking lady. "These are not the latest style, are they? she asked, when the gloves were produced. "Yes, madam," replied the salesman. "We have had them in stock only two days." "I didn't think they were, because the fashion paper says black kids have tan stitches, and vice versa. I see the tan stit.^lle, but not the vice versa." The salesmau exp.ined that vice versa was French for seven but- tons, so she bought three pairs. A QUALIFICATION FOR A KINSMAN.—.Sir Nicholas Bacon being once in the capacity of judge on the point of passing sentence upon a fellow just found guilty of a robbery, the culprit greatly importuned him to save his life ; and, among other things, alleged he had the honour of being one of his lord- ship's relations. "How do you prove that?" mud Sir Nicholas. "My lord," replied the man, "yo' name is Bacon and my name is Hog, and hog and bacon have in all ages been reckoned akin."— " That is true," answered the judge; "but hog is never bacon till it has been hung, and therefore, until you are hung, you can be no relation of mine."

"He's not so wonderful after all," said one of the fair sex; "I have a friend who imitated • the singing of a nightingale so perfectly that a poet living in the next house wrote poems in its honour." "That's nothing to what my friend can do," exclaimed the low comedian, anxious to out-do his 'colleagues, "he imitated the crowing of a cock to -*such perfection in Nice one night, that even nature was taken in, and the sun began to rise although it was evening. The murder of Mr. Wolff Joel in Johannesburg did Rot throw the mining market into the panic that might have been expected. Mr. Joel was the nephew of the late Mr. Barney Barnato, and went out a couple of months ago to Johannesburg to look after the immense interests of the property in which his deceased uncle and his own firm were in- terested. He was a young man of great energy and and part of his mission to Johannesburg was to resuscitate some of the mines which the troubles in the Transvaal had induced his uncle to shut down. His death will delay the plans of his firm, but it is doubtful if, in the present state of the Transvaal,he could have done much to put some of the Barnato group of mines upon their feet.

Mr. Steadman made a novel debut in the House of Commons the other night, by appearing at the table to be sworn before the comm ncement of public business. He maintained his character as an original by taking a short cut from a front bench to a back one. The hon member espied Mr. Misddison behind him, and wishing to engage in conversation clambered over the back of the seat instead of taking the usual, though circuitous, course of walking round. It is believed that this has never been done before in the House ot Com- mons. Staid old members observed the incident in 3ilent horror. For once indignation was frozen into dumb amazement.

The present Government have had a succession of the most surprising surpluses which could have fallen to the lot of a Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the estimate of four millions, which is accepted as the probable surplus for the present year, would at one time have made the nation look forward to a large remission of taxation. Nobody is looking forward to any such relief in the forthcoming Bud- get. Great part of the four millions is pretty well mortgaged or bespeken, and the question of the re • duction of the income tax, or of any other relief to the taxpayers, is at present out of the domain of practical politics. Thus is all very well while the tide of good fortune is Rowing, but. the nation has a right to complain that we are piling liabilities on our head which the taxpayers will be unable to meet in ths event of a turn in the wheel of fortune. A deficit instead of a surplus of four millions would produce fiscal consequences of the most distressing character among classes who were in no sense sharers in the prosperity of the fat yeats.

There is no longer any doubt that Lord Salle- hury's health is causing the gravest anxiety to his colleagues. llpto the present attempts have been made to maintain official secrecy ix the matter, but this policy is now abandoned. At the Foreign Office itself it is freely admitted that the Prime Minister is ao longer equal to the burden which the direction of foreign affairs entails, and he is bound to go ' abroad,in the hope that the change may help to re- store his failing strength. Everybody will share in this hope,espeeially as it is well-known that do- ?antis anxieties are pressing heavily on the Prime Minister. Lady Salisbury's health is, to say the least,unsatisfactory ; and when,in conjunction with this,it is remembered that as Foreign Secretary Lord Salisbury has at the present moment to deal with an unprecedented accumulation of difficult questions,it will be universally felt that his position is one which demands the warmest sympathy.

The newest musical prodigy hails from Australia, where he was born. But he is not a product of. the Anglo-Saxon race, and hears a name which might belong to any of the peoples who make up the curious conglomerate of the Austrian Empire. His father was at one time a Viennese violinist, and the lad, who is eleven years of age, has been the tender object of parental coaching alone. le is of great prococity and of executive genius, and a few con- certs in London will put him in possession of ..the funds which are wanted to enable his musical education to be continued.

I hear that Mr. Gladstone has written a letter to Mr. Dillon which will be read at the '9B St. Patrick's Day. Mr. Gladstone, naturally, does not make any reference to the celebration of the rebellion of '9B, but, confining himself to the pre- banquet on pont problem of practical politics, he once more re- minds Irishmen of all parties that with Ireland di- vided the cause of Home Rule is hopeless, but that with Irel6.nd of one mind and of one spirit the cau;e would be irresistible. This is his message, and it is conveyed with some touching expressioas of personal esteem for Mr. Dillon. The banquet it- self promisee to be a remarkable demonstration, hundreds of applications for tickets having neces- sarily been refused.

div.head: CHAPTER XVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVII.

For hours fog and rain had contended or supre- macy. It had been a miserable day, even for the dreary month of December. Dennis Vane was out of town, and Grace was spending the evening alone. She missed his congenial society, for latterly their tastes had begun to assimilate, and mutual interests were drawing them together. His old friends were rallying round them, and "the Vanes" were now generally spoken of as people who held a rising position in society. Dennis was proud of his pretty wife, and gratified at the attention and admiration she invariably received. Two letters had just arrived. One was from Mrs. llnghes, and contained a graphic, though confused, account of her own doings and the condi- tion of the parish. The other was a short, concise, anxiety-allaying letter from Dennis—exactly the style of letter which nervous wives enjoy receiving from absent husbands. Grace replaced them in their envelopes, then took up the book she was reading. "A man has come to see you, mum," said the parlourmaid, entering. "I told him that I did not think you would like being disturbed; but he says that what he has called about is most particular, and would you please see him, mum." "What is his name ? " asked Grace.
"He said he'd rather not say, but that he's well known to you." "What is he like? "

"Tall and fair. respectable-looking, He doesn't seem as if he'd go away without your seeing him, mum." "Show him upstairs." With a troubled look of apprehension Gruel glanced towards the door. As the man entered he discerned, intuitively, that he was an unwelcome visitor; but he did not seem the least disconcerted thereby. Much to the maid's surprise, he walked up to her mistress and shook hands with the air of an old friend.

"Why have you come to see me? Has anything happened ? " asked Grace anxiously, the moment they were alone. "Oh, no! There's nothing to be especially alarmed about," he answered reassuringly, taking a chair near hers.

"I - was a rat —perhaps—it had been traced—you know what." "No; it hasn't been traced yet. But the police seem to be getting on the right tack. I just called round to talk about what's best to do. You and I—we don't want to be dragged into a lot of trouble. There are others, too, who wouldn't like it any better than we should. I heard that Vane was out of town, so I thought I'd better make the most of this chance of finding you alone." Then, suddenly changing the conversation, as if struck with the style of his surroundings, he added: "You've got a nice home, and I hope you're happy." "Yee," murmured Grace. "But what have you come to suggest? Is there anything I can do to stop the matter being disclosed?" "Yes; of course there is. You must speak up frankly to Vane and tell him all. You've kept the secret from him much too long already. He must be told the moment he gets home." "I cannot tell him! I hoped you had found a way out of the difficulty without his having to know."
" There is no other way. He must be told, and you are the best person to tell him." "I cannot tell him. I cannot make him hate me. Please do tot stay. Someone might corns in, and—"

"I'm beginning to think I shall have to explain matters to Vane myself," he remarked, calmly interrupting her. "Oh! no—no! You—Richard Musgrove—you cannot! you mustn't!" "You can't let things go on as they are now! It's madness! There's a lot of danger for us both in it. Besides, Vane would be twice as wild about the affair if he heard it from a third person. You should speak up straight to him." Grace shuddered and shook her head. "I grant you it will not be pleasant thing to do, but there's no doubt it'll be the safest and best in the end.' "I have tried to tell him, but I cannot," she murmured.

"Have another try," said Musgrove encourag- ingly. "Once you've told him, and got it off your mind, you'll feel better. I hear he's a very proud kind of man—just the sort a,s would feel awfully mad at having his name dragged before the public. You'd better let me tell him if you can't. He'll have to know sooner or later. Now's the best time—before any more harm can be done by stirring up matters." "But what could he do?" -
"Stop things now, before they get nearer finding out the truth."
"Is—is the truth suspected? " gasped Grace in horror.

"No; but there's no knowing how soon it may be. So if you don't tell your husband, and put a spoke in the wheel, I shall." "No—no; you will not be so unkind "—she spoke entreatingly— 'you will do nothing precipitately. There is no immediate hurry." "I'll do nothing that'll make you unhappy," he answered quickly. He could not withstand her pleading eyes. Grace coloured and turned away. "If I were not so poor," he continued, "I'd leave England, change my name, and lie quiet in America for a few years. That is, if it'ud be any help to you." "Are you poor?" she asked suddenly, looking at him.

"Yes, unpleasantly poor." "I would like to help you. To be poor is so dreadful. No one likes you or respects you. Poverty is a kind of crime in the world's eyes. I can easily give you some money." She drew her purse out and opened it. "Would five pounds be of any use to you? " "Thanks—yes " As Musgrove's eyes rested on the five-pound note his face glowed with pleasant surprise. Then he glanced at Grace. "I'm glad you're rich—and happy," he said with a jerk. "Thank you, she answered briefly, handing him the five-pound note. After a pause she added, speaking more calmly: "You'll promise not to tell Mr. Vane anything now? Thank you for wishing to help me, but I would rather no one assisted me."

"I chcln't know that you looked upon this "—he held th, note up—"as a buy off for silence. I didn't e( roe with any intention of asking for it. I'd rather not take it, for some things. But hungry people can't be over-particular. You know what a temptation money is to poor people." "Yes—yes, I know. It is all dreadful— poverty, I mean. But people ought not to do wicked things because they are rioor ; they ought to face their poverty bravely and work hard—but I'm not brave."

Yes, and that's the very reason I don't want you to run the chance of losing this comfortable home. There was a time "—here his voice became low and husky—"when I trusted and hoped I'd be able to give you such a home, but luck was against me. I haven't a brass farthing to bless myself with now."

Grace coloured painfully during these last remarks, and decided that it was her duty to cut the interview short. "Are you homeless ? " she asked. "No—thank heaven—not yet." .She rose. Musgrove knew it was a signal for his departure. The usual inconsistency of his mind led him to resent this manner of suggesting he should go. In days gone by he had loved Grace ardently; and he loved her still, though he knew she regarded him with pity mingled with rear. Now they shared together the secret that was undermining her happiness, and he had it in his power to rob her of Dennis's love by disclosing that secret to him, in an unfavourable light. Musgrove knew the strength of his position. It gave birth to a feeling of obstinacy, and he retained his seat with the utmost sangfroid. "You do not appear very hospitably inclined," said he, glancing at the tea-tray. "But you cannot think that I have treated you unkindly," she answered, in a half-apologetio manner.

"Oh, no!" His thoughts reverted to the five-pound note, and he rose with a feeling of compunction. "You'll act sensibly, I hope, Grace, and tell Vane all about that transaction. It'll be a bad day's work for you and me if he finds it out from another source. He'll be furiously angry with you for having kept it dark. He's not a fool. He'd rather have .it out with you in Titivate than

div.head: CHAPTER XVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVIII.

It was now the first week IA May, and Londoners were just launching out into their usual May-time gaieties. Invitations for "At Homes " were daily arriving for the Vanes. It happened that Dennis had just reached that degree of eminence which ensures being talked about, in consequence of his masterly defence of a man falsely aecused of .nurder.

There was however, an idea prevalent amongst Vane's friends that hard work and success did not suit him, as, instead of' his continuing to be a congenial companion, he was daily becoming less sociable. More than once Eric Hume had chaffed him for labouring under •an attack of "chronic blues."
"Vane must be making a pile of money," observed their mutual friend, Charles Troup, one evening when be chanced to drop in for a quiet pipe with Eric.

"Yes, he must be; and I'm rattling glad of it. Considering how hard lie works, he ought to make money. I/ wish he didn't age so fast, though. He's positively growing bald!" " ,‘!So I noticed the other day. He looks as if he had forsworn all fun in life. Work—work— work is all he goes in for now. Nothing would induce me to slave away as he does. I often wonder how he gets on with his wife. Queer thing—that marriage of his! I thought Vane had a lot too much aomnion-sense to rush into matri- mony in such a hurry." "His marriage belongs to ancient history," said Eric pointedly. "Yes; :they have been married: for sometime now. She is awfnlly pretty, but too quiet. I don't care for that style of woman." "I think she's strikingly pretty. Here is such a classical, refined kind of ,beauty," said Eric. "There's too much al the china °Timmer* element in her beauty to please me. I admirb some go ' and vivacity about a woman. There's something so monotonously pleasing in her." Eric meditatively knocked off the end of his cigar, then, abruptly changing the conversation, observed:
. "It's an odd thing that the person who forged Vane's name to that cheque has never been d iscovered.

"Yes, very," concurred the- other. "I suppose it will never be known now. It must be eight months since Vane found it out. The police do not seem to have taken the matter up very ener- getically." "They haven't completed their investigations yet. Between you and me, I'm afraid the matter will be brought home nearer to Vane than he expects." "Why? asked asked the other eagerly. "Don't know exactly—can't explain somehow," was the evasive answer. "If you suspect that, why don't you give him the tip to stop matters being pushed any further ? " "I tried to do so one day, and I saw he did not care about my advising him. Of course, he didn't understand what I was driving at." "Naturally not. I believe his wife's father was an awful old scoundrel—bad lot altogether." "I never heard much about him, and of course I never cared to inquire. I'm very glad that the wedding is turning out as well as it is. Vane is an out-and-out good fellow, and deserves all the luck possible. If his wife comes of a bad lot,' then all the more credit is due to her for being as nice as she is."

"There is a great deal in what you say. Any- how, I'm glad I'm not in Vane's shoes." Eric made no reply, but he mentally echoed his friend's sentiments,. "I was at the Royal Academy yesterday," said Troup after a short pause, and saw Miss Treherne's picture, Hope's Achievement.' It well deserves all the praise it has received. It's a most successful work—shews much power and imagination. The tone of the colouring is admir- able." "There's no doubt it is one of the most success- ful pictures of the year." "Quite thr most successful amongst the rising artists, so I h ,uld say." "Yes; every detail is so well finished and care- fully thought out. There's nothing slurred about the work. As to the centre figures, I know for a fact that she painted Hope's face eleven times before she was satisfied with it. Her powers of perseverance are extraordinary—at least, they appear so to me. But I suppose the majority of successful artists possess an equal amount of plodding powers." "Yes; but whenever a woman has a hobby she goes in for it might and main. I was told that Miss Treherne works morning, noon and—l was going to add—night. But I suppose she doesn't slave away quite so hard, does she? " "She works hard, there's no doubt of it. But now that she has got a picture ' on the line,' she will probably take matters more easily. She is one of those girls who will do everything well that they attempt." "And she is a great favourite in society. She is lucky It is not every girl's fate to be clever, successful, beautiful and rich."

"No, it isn't," Eric concurred. "That reminds me that some friends of mine, who were at Les Ac-ants last year, tell me that everyone there believed she and Vane were either already engaged or else on the verge of becoming so. When I told them he had married someone else they would scarcely believe me." "People are so fond of jumping to conclusions, especially with regard to love affairs," was the casually-spoken reply. "I expect you could a tale unfold if you chose to do so. However, I'm not the least surprised to hear that Vane was hit' in that direction. There is scarcely a fellow in London, as you know, who does not admire Miss Treherne, either com- paratively or superlatively." "You are too observant by half," said Eric, with an amused laugh. Ile liked to hear his future sister-in-law eulogised. Then he added: "She is one of the best of daughters and best of sisters. That I know for a positive fact." "A fellow who could marry a milk-and-water, scared-looking mortal like Mrs. Vane could never have appreciated a brilliantly clever girl like Miss Treherne ; so it was a lucky escape for the latter that Vane's admiration cooled down. Perhaps she refused him."

"Perhaps so," was the diplomatic rejoinder. But, as we know, this by no means represented Gwendoline's own thoughts on the subject. Dis- appointment and a heavy heart lay beneath hes merry laugh and bright, animated conversation. That time at Les Avants still hovered in her mind as the happiest in her life. It was to deaden the recollection of it that she now worked with untiring energy. Once only had she seen Dennis since her return to London; then she had been distressed to notice how fast'he was ageing. Meanwhile, as she often told "'Constance, she was becoming more and snore enamoured of a spinster's existence. "I will renounce to you the pleasure of rejoicing mother's heart with providing a family wedding, she said, a few days after the Private View at the Royal Academy, when Constance called in at the studio.

These views by no means coincided with Mrs. Treherne's matrimonial aspirations on behalf of her daughters. Both were to marry, and to marry well; so she had decided years ago. She liked Eric Hume very much—especially now that he was .recognised as a rich wide 's heir. That qwendoline, her talented and greatly admired daughter, should remain single was a contingency that she did not consider possible. From the moment she returned home on varnishing day with the news that her picture had been hung on the line Mrs. Treherne had decided that her elder daughter's husband ought to be a very exalted personage, and a rich young peer now flitted before her mind as a possible son-in-law. But she had wisely refrained from unburdening her mind to Clwendoline on the subject. It was to Mr. Treherne alone that she mentioned the matter. He, wise man, though unable, and probably un- wishful, to • understand her aspirations, refrained from saying anything definite. "Henry, :brill live to be very proud of our e htl'tus Insticallv one evenina.
CHAPTER XIX. Gwendoline Treherne has been _arrested "

!fir c-Ilu-n;e burst into Dennis Vane's ellamners with these words on his lips. "Arrestedl-41iss Treherne arrested! Are yott mad? " was the sharply-spoken reply. '!Mad-:-he! I was never more sane in all my life!" ."But what has she been arrested for ? "
"For uttering that forged cheque of yours! * "Uttering —that forged cheque!" repeated. Dennis in blank dismay. "Its. a sheer impossibility 1 Some terrible and unpardonable mistake has been made ".
you know nothing about It? "queried Erie. "Of course I don't!" thundered Dennis. "Did you imagine I had acted such an infamous part as to _cause her to be arrested ? "

"To me it did not seem possible." "I should take it as a deliberate insult if you did think it possible But are you absolutelr certain that Miss Treherne has been arrested?" "Yes—absolutely certain. She was arrested this afternoon at her studio and taken to Bow Street. I have seen her there." "The police must have confused her with some- one else or—or there has been some false evidence offered them. She must be perfectly innocent of the charge." "Of course she must be. But that does not alter matters. She has been arrested, and will be taken before the magistrate to-morrow charged with uttering that forged cheque of yours." "D— that cheque! " ejaculated Dennis, bring- ing his fist down on the table. "Then she is at Bow Street now? " "Yes. I was there an hour ago. I went home with Mr. Treherne, and then came straight on to you." "How does she bear it all?" The question way asked in a husky voice. "Splendidly ! By Jingo, she has pluck! She behaved with a coolness and dignity that fairly astonished the police." "Poor girl—poor girl!" murmured Dennis, springing to his feet and beginning to pace up and down the room. His hands moved nervously, and he was ghastly pale. "But the police cannot possibly possess evidence that can bring the charge home to her! " he continued with growing indig- nation. "It's a radical impossibility " "You're right. Yet they evidently think they possess very strong evidence against her. Sir Henry Hilton signed the warrant, and, as you know, he is one of the last men to sign one without weighty evidence being placed before him. Then he knows Miss Treherne's position, and cannot fail to comprehend the gravity of allowing such 6 charge to be brought against one, who occupies a uniquely, prominent position at the present moment." _

"That is only too true. Hilton is one of the most cautious magistrates we have. It is quite certain he would not have signed that warrant unless he believes the charge can be supported." "Supported by perjured evidence it certainly' can be." Eric spoke more calmly now, but with increased bitterness.

...... Dennis leant back meditatively for es fele minutes, then said. "My opinion is this—speaking from what I know of Miss Treherne and the impossibility of her having uttered this cheque—l fully believe that some culpable mistake has been made by the police, which a few words of explanation will put right.' "Lot us hope so. However, no more can be done in the matter until to-morrow."

"I suppose you will brief the ex-Attorney General? I should strongly advise it ? " "I will suggest his name to Mr. Treherne. But I wish you would come back with me to Queen Anne's Gate, and give us the benefit of youv advice!'

"Would Mr. Treherne care- about seeing me under the circumstances?" asked Dennis witb hesitation. "Yes 7 I am sure he would take it as an appro- priate act of courtesy, and it would make him feel doubly certain that you thoroughly believe in his daughter's innocence. "Then I'll come with you, and advise you to the best of my ability." "Thanks, old man; we- all know that yous advice is worth haying. Both Mr. and Mrs. rreherne asked me if I thought you had anything to do with Gwen's arrest, and I said I was posi- tive you had not. It would be as well for you emphatically to deny all knowledge of the mattes to them, if occasion offers." "I will certainly do so. I cannot tell you how much I regret not having, failed to discover thal that cheque was forged. When you rushed in just now and told me that Miss Treherne had been arrested for uttering it, I was thunderstruck." "You looked it. Can you come with me at once? I promised Mr. Treherne I would return as soon as possible." "I'm ready now," answered Dennis, locking his desk. "I only wish it were in my power to stop the prosecution; but unfortunately it is not." "I see you are awfully cut up about the matter." said Eric. "I am indeed avwfully cut "—He checked him- self abruptly, then added: "Miss Treherne's posi- tion is a cruelly hard .one. This morning she was one of the greatest favourites in society, against whom nobody had ever breathed a word; and in an hour's time her name will appear in every evening paper connected with a crime of which she is wholly and entirely innocent. The whole calamity is traceable to me and to my cheque. I tell you, Hume, in confidence "—he lowered his voice, which noir trembled with emotion—"that there is no human being for whom I would more willingly have sacrificed my life to save from trouble—yet— yet— My God! it's too terrible to think of!" "There's no use, old man, in dilating on these miseries. It only makes one feel madly angry, and is of no practical use," said Eric kindly. "Besides, we're wasting valuable time. Come, I must be off." As he spoke he took up his hat and moved towards the door. Dennis rose and followed him in silence. A few minutes later they were driving in the direc- tion of Queen Anne's Gate. "If we do not succeed in breaking up the prose- cution to-morrow, we shall at least succeed in getting bail," said Eric, as they drew up at the Trehernes' house. "Meanwhile, I hope you'll do your level best to raise Mr. Treherne's spirits. I'm afraid the affair will nearly kill him.' They found him pacing the library in a distress- ing condition of apprehension. He looked anxiously towards them as they entered, and Dennis noticed with a pang of compunction that already there were new lines of care on his face.

"As I anticipated, Vane knows nothing of the prosecution," observed Eric. "He had not even heard of the arrest until I told him half an hour ago." "Then we are as much in the dark as before," ' replied Mr. Treherne. "Yes, and must remain so until after the hear- ing to-morrow." "I was greatly pained and annoyed when Hume told me what had happened," observed Dennis. "I am wholly at a loss to understand on what runds the police have instituted these proceedings. is impossible for them to possess trustworthy evidence in support of the prosecution." "I am glad to hear you express those view., Vane," said Mr. Treherne, speaking a degree more cheerfully. "I did not think you could be implicated in the prosecution—of:, more correctly speaking, persecution—of my daughter." "I shall be glad if I can be of any assistance in bringing forward evidence in Miss Treherne'n favour. I shall be heartily glad when her innocence is proved, as of course it will be." ' "Thank you," replied Mr. Treherne warmly. "The whole affair has burst upon us with such cruel suddenness that at the present moment I feel ' almost stunned with grief—and humiliation."._

said the Ism. in a low lame, then, raising again, cm:tinned: "I sin speaking openly to you. Fan,, for I mu sure you fe,2.1 for us." "I do indeed—most keen iv." cc Ai f•jr nly ConsLanee. the. ale atiAvly
Ire ceased speaking, for at that moment Mrs. Treherne entered hurriedly. Passing Dennis with- out taking any notice of him, she asked her husband in a troubled voice:

"Has Mr. Vane been able to explain satisfac- torily his cruel conduct to dear Gwendoline ? " Dennis coloured and walked to the window. "You must exonerate Vane from all blame, Mary," expostulated her husband. "He is as ignorant of the grounds on which she has ' been arrested as you or I, and he feels deeply both for us and Gwendoline. He has kindly offered to assist us in bringing forward evidence in her favour."

"Really! That is very good and thoughtful of you." Saying this Mrs. Treherno turned to Dennis and shook hands in a conciliatory manner. "I suppose it is quite in your power to check the prosecution at once ? " she added. "Unfortunately it does not lie in my power to do so," replied Dennis with hesitation. "The matter is in the hands of my bankers, Messrs. Hanks and Co., and has gone too far for my interference to be of any good. If the affair were hushed "up a the'present juncture a fatal,. mistake would be made."

Mrs. Treherne sank into a chair and gazed before her in blank despair. Suddenly, however, her expression changed, and she looked up eagerly at Dennis. "You can at least,"., she began impres- sively, "write to all the newspapers and say that though my daughter has been prosecuted for utter- ing a cheque to which ~-our name was forged, you know for certain that she is ;absolutely innocent. A letter ,from you would read so appropriately, and it would allay all unpleasant gossip." As she finished speaking she glanced round in a manner that clearly inferred she expected to be supported in this suggestion. "People-are not allowed to express their opinions publicly on trials that are pending," said her husband. "Mr. Vane could not do as you request." . "But, Henry, I am thinking of our dear.child's good—not of what people are 'allowed• to do. Ifothing interests me but our dear Gwendoline's happiness. If once people believe her guilty they will continue doing so for over. Now is the moment for us to step forward and state that she is innocent. You know how easily the public mind is biassed. No one should be -allowed to imagine that she is guilty." "We can do nothing'to influence publio opinion, Mary—it is impossible " "Mrs. Treherne, I would most willingly do as you suggest," observed Dennis, "if it were possible. Unfortunately it is not." "Then am I to understand that you are all going to stand by inactively, and allow people to say cruel'and unjustifiable things of my beautiful and talented daughter ? " indignantly demanded Mrs. Treherne.

"Unfortunately, our hands are tied in the matter.", jler,husband spoke-hopelessly. "Dq_y_ou not agree with my suggestions; Eric?" asked Mrs. Treherne, addressing him for the first time. "The only course open to us is to engage the most talented counsel of the day to defend Gwendoline " was the evasive reply. "If you are going to talk about law and lawyers, I cannot stay and listen. It is not as if Gwendo- line would have to face a regular trial before a judge and jury." The three men glanced at each other, but said nothing. "This is what I suggest,' continued Mrs. Treherne, trying to sfieak forcibly, "that all the members of her family and her' intimate friends join together and state openly,- before the world at large, that she is innocent" With these words Mrs. Treherne glanced from one to the other of her listeners, happily ignorant, that her meaning was not quite clear. Mr. Treherne merely shook his head, and neither Dennis nor Eric made any remark. "I must leave you. I cannot stand the strain of ordinary con- versation," she observed, rising and moving towards the door. "But before going I must implore yon, Henry, to endeavour to keep your daughter's good name unsullied from association with—with the police-court. Somebody must take the initiative and tell our friends that she is being prosecuted by mistake. I sent off this morning three hundred invitations for an At HOTTIP. Everyone will decline if they think Gwendoline is—er—being de- rja tamed—" Here the poor lady sank down and began sobbing violently. "The At Home must be put off!" said her husband decisively; "and, Mary, cannot you see how acutely all this pains me and prevents my arranging as to our immediate course of action." Mr. Treherne placed his hand soothingly on hers. "I am grieved for you—and us all; but we must not waste time in useless regrets. The first hear- ing before the magistrate will be on to-morrow. Vane and Hume have come to talk matters over with me."
F
t

"Very well; I will go, then. Promise me you will act for the best, Henry ? " "Can you doubt it ? " he said in a pained voice. "I should like to tell you, Mrs. Treherne, before you go, that I intend offering myself as bail to-morrow," said Dennis. "This will show publicly my belief in your daughter's innocence. Everyone will know that I am of opinion she is being erroneously prosecuted." "Thank you—thank you," murmured Mn. Tzeherne gratefully, between her sobs. Under the circumstances her departure pro- duced a feeling of relief. Dennis at once brought his acute legal mind to bear on the subject of Gwendoline's arrest. But, considering the specti• lathe nature of his reasonings, no tangible advice was possible. Mr. Treherne drew his chair near the table, and entered in his notebook matten on which the younger men wanted him to gain infor- Bastion from Gwendoline. Then counsel were discussed, and it was arranged that Eric should brief the ex-Attorney-Genus's Sir Edward .Masters.

Al? Dun NELLIE. The hats to be worn during the spring and summer are very gorgeous. Their shapes are either made of drawn glace silk or of satin straw. The ended quills of yesteryear have been im- proved by a fringe of ostrich feathers on one side and a black hat is indispensable to the possessions of every well-dressed woman. Bright violet straw is popular, pale blue straw is popular, and a curious feature of the new hats is a high round crown, which towers above a curled brim and is decorated at either side with an ostrich feather,

the base of these feathers being - by a scarf of glaed eilk buckled with Parisian diamond buckles. And, talking of Parisian diamond buckles, I must observe and exclaim upon the exceeding charms of the new combs of Spanish .outline, when they are of very light tortoiseshell and com- pletely covered with a very fine trellis of diamond work. Al! the elegant women are Wearing these, and they fill with much discretion the space at the base of the coil of hair which continues to rest high up on our crowns. Afternoon gowns of faced cloth in light shades with dark silk or velvet are exceedingly fashion- able, and many of the gowns worn at recent smart weddings have been in this style. COMMITrEE.

A special meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall,War- rington, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Wright) presided, and there were also present Alderman FaireloiNli, Alderman Rolton, Alderman Hutchinson, Councillors U. Roberts. F R. Roberts, John Roberts, William Pierpoint, J. Soaw Green, G. Plumpton, J. Smothurst„l. Eine,J. E, isn't, W. Furness, J. Grace, A. Jolley,Rogers, J. Shillcock, Wilkinson,A. Woods, D. T in- nion,A. Peacock, J. Lee, flcaton, Burton, Dr. Cannel!, with Mrssrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town cler!<). J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer). Dr. Gornall (medical officer of health). T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Stanley Wilson (depaty town clerk), and W. -S. Haddock (gas engineer). THE MAYOR'S VISIT TO WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

Councillor 11. ROIMRI43 said.: Before proceeding with the resolution which is down in my name, may I, with the permission of the Council, perform what is to my- self an exceedingly pleasing duty, ansi it is on behalf of my Nonconformist colleagues in this Council,on my own behalf, and also in the name of the whole Dissenting community, to thank you Mr.Mayor,for having as Cnief Magistrate of this borough recognised a large section of your fellow townsmen by attending Divine service at Wycliffe Church two Sundays ago. Your action has, I am confident, had the warm -approval of all the more intelligent and broad-minded of your fellow Churchmen, and has largely won for you the affection and regard of that section of the community to which I sin proud to belong. I also desire, at the same time, to tender my thanks to those of my colleagues, and other townsmen, who, like yourself,belong to the Established Church,and who accompanied y•mu on the occasion in question, and to express the hope that the better feeling whieh exists amongst the members of the Corporation may be fostered and-extended by acts of courtesy similar to that which you have so happily initiated. The MAYOR said it gave him great pleasure to attend Wycliffe Church, and he was extremely pleased both with the service and the sermon. (Hear. hear.) When he accepted Oise, as they knew he did somewhat re- luctantly, he made up his mind to he Mayor of the whole town, and not a part of it. (Hear, hear.) Every- one knew that he was a staunch Churchman, and he stili remained so, but he still had great sympathy with other Christian bodies. (Hear, hear, and applause).
THE GAS COMMITTE'E FURTHER INFORMATION REQUIRED.

Councillor HENRY ROBERTS than moved the following reselution :—" That the Gas Committee be instructed to furnish a report to the Council showing—the amount of money charged in the cost of the manufacture of gas for—(a)all renewals any repairs rendered necessary by ordinary wear and tear; (b), all renewals or replace- ments caused by any other circumstances (the causes of such renewals or replacements to be sst out in the report) ; (e), all additions to plant, mains, or buildings, temporary or permanent. The report to cover the period from January lit, 1890, to December 31st, 1897, and to show the costeseparately for each year." He said he wished it to be distinctly understood that the object of this resolution was not in any sense to make an attack of a personal character either upon the committee slr upon any official.under their control. The sole purpele which he had in view was to prevent the continuance lof a policy which, if his deductions from the Gas En- gineer's report were correct, was manifestly unfair to the present ratepayers, was unwise from 'a financial point of view, and was calculated to create suspicions AS to the true condition of things which would net otherwise arise. The gas works had been the property of the Corpse. ation now for about 20 years. When it WAS originally purchased it was anticipated that it would speedily be- come a source of .material help to the rates of the borough, by means of large annual contributions froto the profits of gas making, and ' which should he been contributed to the improvement rate account. Tile contributions up to the present had been most disap- pointing, and by no means representative of what the profits during the past 20 years should have been. it was true that there had been some reduction in the price of gas and in the charge for street lighting, and that altogether comething like £4,000 had been contributed in relief of the rates; but the sum total of these contribti- lions had been infinitesimal compared with what was anticipated, and what ought to have been made. The question then arose—why had the beneficial contribu- tions been so paltry? Did the manufacture of gas cost more in Warrington than in otherplacec ? That it did not was shown by the analysis of the cost of mannfac. ture as set out in Mr. HaddockOi report for the year 1889-90. On page 13 of that report he found that in the year 1889 the cost of manufacture as dis- tinguished from the statutable charges payable by the Corporation on capital and interest account came to 17•24 d. per thousand cubic feet and in the year 1890 to 18.57 d. These years he took to be normal in regard to the expense, and the cost to be the average cost of manufacture. If the Council would now follow the re- port they would See that the cost of manufacture jumped up from 17d. per thousand feet 1889 to 20fd...- in 1891, 24. in 1894. It was 21d. in 1298; 2211 in 1896, and 23-0. in 1897. The small and apparently insignifioant sum of one Donny per thousand cubic feet on the total quantity of gas /manufactured amounted te more than £l,OOO. The extra cost of gas manufacture in the veers 1891 to 1897, therefore came out as follovra :-1891, £3,250; 1892, '3,250; 1893, £7,250 ; 1894, £7,500; 1895, £4,000; 1899, £5,500 ; 1897, £6,500. Or, in other words, the gross total of the extra cost of gas-making over and above the average normal cod during the years 1891 to 1897 amounted to £37,200. If this large sum of money were all that had to be accounted for it would be sufficiently serious to justify the present motion ; but time was a yet further sum of money to be taken into account. The statutable charges of the Corporation—which meant the repayment of principal and interest, or, in other words, thei capital debt of the Corporation on gas works account amounted to on an average yearly 1311. per thousand etrbic feet for the years 1889-90-91. The charges then became lower through the repayment of principal, and the consequent deduction of the amount on interest an nuatly to be paid, cod for the years 1892-3 4-5-6-1 the figures were 131, 11d., 10d., 11d., 11d.,103., and 9d. He cha not, of course, pledge himself to the absolute accuracy of the figures, hut they represented the facts as nearlr as could he ascertained from the engineer's re- port. Now, what was the explanation of this extra- ordinary condition of things? The only solution that suggested indeihtaserlzftog his mind was that the Gas Committee d b against the cost of gas manufacture a very large portion of the sum he had arrived at, and which ought to have been charged to capital, tie ad- mitted that so far as the cost of removal from Mersey- street to Longford was concerned the greater portion of that might properly and legitimately be charged against revenue, but in the absence of any definite Information thecae°. as to the amount of money involved, he was not able to express a decided opinion. But probably one effect of the -resolution would be to enable the Council to be supplied with the figures relative to this particular item of expen- diture, In proof of the inference t hat he ha 4 drawn he found that while in 1893 a loin of £20,000 WAS sanc- tioned by the Local Government Board, and afterwards obtained, over £4,000 of that menev hid not yet been tak.n up. This should have besn utilized by the Gas Committee instead of absorbing that emouot from revenue account. Again, in Jun, 1897, the committee came to the Council with a application Co borrow £lO,OOO for the purpose of slo", remelts and £20,000 for gas works extensions. The first part of the resolution, referring tin the purchase of slot meters, was approved and adopted by the Council. The second part, referring to the loan of £20,000 for extensions, was referred back by the Council to the Committee for the production. of estimates and leans. From that date until now nol further communication had been made by the Gas Com- mittee to the Council in reference to this proposed loan. Either the loan was required or it was not required. If it was required in June 1897, surely it was still necessary for the purpose of extensions. If it was net required in June, 1897, it ought not to have been asked for. The conclusion he had come to in regard to this particular loan, was that the money had been Pro- vided from other seurcesor, in other words, the exten- sions had been made a charge against the revenue ac- count, instead of against capital. In further proof of thisef the Council would refer again to the report, On 1 page six ther would find that under the item " Repairs of iron and brickwork "there had been an enermous in- crease of expenditure. Taking the average of 1889-90 the expenses under this bee 1 amounted to less than 2d., per thousand cubic feet. The increase in the following veer on this item alone name not as follows :-1891, £3,750 ; 1892,21,250 ; 1893,0.750 ; 1894, £5,250 ; 1895, £3,500; 1898, £4,750; 1897, £5,500; or a total of £27,700 under this one heed lie did not suppose any member of the Council would believe that such an abnormal Con- dition of things hi been hreught about by fair wear and tear. He confessed that the item was not candid when such large sums were attributed to re ,airs of iron and brick work.

If he was right in assuming that this had been and was still the policy of the Gas Committee, then with all re- spect he unhesitatingly asserted that their policy was not only manifestly unfair to the ratepayer of to-day, but was also illegal. (Hear, hear.) The Gas Act pro- vided, after setting forth the various items which might be charged against the gas mannfacturer,that its income should be charged in payment of the working and establishmmt expense., and the cost of maintenance of their gas undertaking. and the cost )f collection and re- covery of gas rents. But there was no provision there for any charge which was of the nature of an extension of or an addition to either the plant or works being made against revenue. Finally the Gas Act provided that after the various items of cost had been met, none of which provided for the policy whl'h the Gas Commit- tee had been carrying out, that they (the committee) "shall from time to time carry to the improvement rate fund of the borough the net surplus remaining after the fulfilment of the several purposes aforesaid, and the annual proceeds to the reserve fund when the same amounts to £10,000." There was an old saw which said they could not .et butter out of a dog's throat, and it might be imol..ible to recover any serious portion of this round sum of £50,000 which required accounting for by the Gas Committee.
Alderni—an BotroN : You are not entitled to it.

COLIOCiIIOr ROBIERT3 : If yen take that position I shall show you that we are entitled to it. Continuing, 'he said he did not wish for reasons which had been used, to discuss side issues which might be prejedicial to the interests of the Corpora- tion. His purpose wauld be served in a great msasure, and the ratepayers of Warrington would he fairly satisfied, if the Gas Committee would from this time give them their assurance that their future policy at any rate would beguided by a proper and due regard to the interests of the present ratepayer, and that under Ine circumstance would they permit any charge to be made against revenue which could be properly and legally charged against capital. If this policy were pur- sued they would receive from the Gas Committee in aid 11 of rates the RUM of money which in his oninion, from the figures he had carefully considered, ought not to be less than £4,000 or £5,000 par annum. There was no member of the Council who had sym- reathised more with the difficulties which the Gas Committee had had thrown upon its sheulders. He remembered the primary fact that too much money was paid in the bee,inning for the undertaking. They accepted the inevitable fact that they would have to re move from Mersey-street to Longford at some time, bat they never expected to do so so early. They had in front of them as a town some very large and costly im- provements. (Hear, hear.) The sum of money which had been absorbed during the last seven years represen- ted, according to the explanation which the committee might have to give, at the least Si, and at the most 101 in the £to the ratepayers of Warrington. (Hear,hear.) Assuming, as he hoped and believed was the fact, that the Gas Committee had now got over the serious charac- ter of its difficulties, and had got its works into a poei- tion in which it would be able to hand over to them substantial profits in order that the ratepayers wile had pledged their credit for the institution might have antaltantial benefit from it, he believed that the G 35 Committee, if -the past were forgotten, were prepared te tarn over a nee, leaf and give the ratepayers the benefit of the money which was, he coatended, equal to the amount of the profits after certain defined charges. The improvements to which he referred, which were so de- , eirable and so necessare if the progress of the town was to be maintained, eught to he done at the least possible cost to the ratepayers. an in order to bring that about the gasworks, which should he a profitable undertaking, should do it share by makine as much money as it could, and by handing over as much as possible for the benefit of these expenses. (Haar, hear, and apo!ause,) Alderman FLIRCLOI.7taS said he had no objection to secondins.(that resolution, The Gas Committee were willing to have the fullest enquiries possible. They had net robbed the ratepayers of a penny-piece, but had been anxious to put the concern on a really sound basis. It was a rotten concern at one time but it would be one of the best paying concerns in Warrington if the Council would only have a little patience. He was not going to sewer emaneillor Roberts that night, hut after the en-

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MARCH 18, 1898.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MARCH 18, 1898.

q iiry wis ins le thon all would be made public:. He would like to know who was going to furnilh all this information. WWI it likely the their offiaials would fur- nish all the information wanted? It would take nearly Rix wepki,

_ Councillor FURNESS said he would previously have liked to have said something on this matter but a roan- lution to enter into committee was carried and that waa affective in closing up discussion. Ho took it that the effect of the resolution was to stop the Gas Comaaittee frent spending more money without the consent of the Council. Money had been spent by the committee and to a very large extent. He believed the sum total spent came to £52,000 or £53,000. They had had the gas con- cern about 21 years now and the chairman of the Gas Committee asked them to have a little more patience. They had had patience for 21 years eel the result was that they owed almost as much now on the L.Me under- taking—in fact more than when they originally bought the works. (Cries of " No, no.") They had had the concern 21 years and all the committee had gi een them back for an expenditure of almost a quarter of a million had been the paltry sum of £4,000. Such a sum was ve,v m-ag,re and not what they ought to expect. In 1889 it cost the ratepayers practical e per thousand feet for brickworic and r -r. rt; in other years the cost WAS 21., 1 1,. 11, and in 1897 it WAS close upen 70. There was some reason for thia expenditure. PI had not gone in brick-work and wear and tear. 1., moat have been spent on permanent works. He tho iget the Council was justified in asking the Gas Committeeto lay before them, in future, any scheme they might have for extending the works. If they took their expendi- ture out of revenue they gave the Council no chance whatever of exercising its judgment upon the expenses they were making. Their obj'CG was to give the Coun- cil power to either refuse or sanction anv further ex- penditure of money on account of the Gas Works. The MAYOR: Permanent works.

Councillor FURNESS : Yes, I mean permanent works. In 1896, he added,thei actual amount spent on brick and iron work was over £3OOO. In 1897 it was almost double that sum. He thought Councillor Roberts's figures were quite sufficient to show that there must be some extra- ordinary expenditure of money that the Committee ought to give some explanation of. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BOLTON said they could not discuss the matter until they got the facts out. There were always some people who understood your business better than yourself. When they bought a company like the Gas Works 20 years ago with every burden in the nape of loans, they had to let their renewals and expense., go up until they had put it in order. Se far as the motion was concerned, the gas committee with their present staff could not furnish the information in a reasonable time.lf they had asked theTinancepommittee —who muddled the affairs of the Corporation, and who pretended to understand everything—they would have done it. (Laughter). Councillor PIERPOINT said he must take exception to what had been said. He did teink the elder and more learned members of the Corporation should learn a little discretion. If this Council decided that the report had to be oven then it was the duty of the Gas C ommittee to supply it—(hear, hear)—and he believed the Commit- tee would supply it. He was rather inclined to take this Position-6 wear a white sheet as a member of the Gas Committee and acknowledge that he had done wrong. Having done wrong he had done that wrong on the be- half of the gas works, and in the interests of the com- munity. They saw the error of their ways and would endeavour to carry out the principles enunciated so ably by Councillor Roberts. He could say that if wroag had been done it had been done with no intention to inflict injury upon any individual and he was glad that the Council was coming to its senses in criticising the work of committees because he thought there were other com- mittees that they might criticise. There were the doings of the Proportv Purchasing C ern tnittee for instance. If criticisine the Gas Cernmittee would bring anew a eriti- clam of other committees they would not have spent their time in vain. 44 Councillor J. SI:WV GREEN said if it was a fact that the Finance Committee did muddle the affairs of the Corporation it was time they discharged every one of them. Alderman 133LTON : The letting of Victoria Park Is enough. ' Continuing, Councillor &OM GREEN said be did not know how it was there was so much feeling introduced into this question but for some twelve months now several members of the Gas Committee had had an idea that there was some particular reason in his mind for calling upon them to centeibute in 'aid of the rates. He had known of this expenditure for several years, and his attention was called to it some three years ago Ie looking back he found that in 1889 the Gas Committee were kind enough to tell the Council that they had made a profit of £4,441,and he could not account there- fore for the profit shown three years ago being about £lOO, and the investigations which he pursued with the aid of the Berough Treasurer, who was well up in the matter,enabled him to clearly follow the course of the figures Councillor Roberts had given. He did net enter into this with any personal feeling, but here was their position. The Council required the Finance Com- mittee to find them the money they wanted to spend during the year. The Finance Committee had so to speak, to be above all the committees and look down upon them to see whether they could not find that money with the least possible anxiety to the ratepayers. He looked about to See whether some money could not be raised withous increasing the rates of the Borough and he saw very early that the Gas Committee,if they would, could give them the money. Alderman FAIRCLOgUR : And they did. Councillor SELLW Geese, continuing, said that in the name of the Finance Committee he wrote to Alderman Fairclough last year asking them to give £2,000. He pointed out in the letter the information he was in pos- session of and that he knew they could do it. It was done after some pressure. Seeing what they hal to face in the corning year he suggested a few months ago that the committee should give £1,500 and was told by a member of the Gas Committee that he went to the Gas Department with a pistol in his hand demanding the money. It was utterly impassible to do anything mere kindly than the way this was done. Councillor Roberts had shown very distinctly and clearly that instead of giving in aid of the rates that balance of profit which the Act said they should, the Gas Depatt- meat had spent it in capital expenditure. He had known this but he did not object to it. In a reasonable way it was right and proper, but they should not do an jujus- ties to those who were responsible. His opinion was gas, and a substantial sum ia aid of the rates generally, and then leave the Gas Department eufficient to go on adding to their improve- ments out of revenue. He contended that the time had that redtuhcetri reduction ni was n t ahe rate of profit handsome enough to provide for a arrived when the Gas Department should show a debtor and a creditor statement of the assets and liabilities and of the revenue accounts, and he hoped the Council would say that the Gas Department should render a proper and legitimate account at the close of each year. (Hear, hear). Councillor Tleencee said as a member of the Gas Com- mittee he bad not the slightest objection to the resolu- tion or anything' that Csiuncillor Roberts had said, but ht the best thing would be to have the explan- ation out as quickly as possible. His experience of tahhtei ho the got suoWorks was that the explanation could not be got out by the staff in anything like reasonable timeeind he suggested that someone should be appointe I to pre- pare the information. The mater could then be die- cussed,explanatione could be given, and Ise thought the statement when produced would show that it was not that hideous thing which rumour during the last few days had declared it to be. It was simply a question of tmPoyed and more than ' fullyaatc ico onu be g ens. Their tby employed, and he would suggest that the inf arm- yssot na staff was e other e fullyp, r a 0 beside the Gas Com- mittee. Councillor Geece contended that the officials of the Gas Works had tune. Several of the members of the Corporation who knew gas officials knew that they had the time, and that they could place the facts and figures before the Council if they had the books. The increase of the cost of iron and brick work up to 61. per thousand cubic feet seemed to him an abnormal increase. He was told that the big wall surrounding the Longford Gas- works was paid for out of the revenue instead of capital. He thought it was a mistake to charge the present day ratepayere with an enormous expenditure which pos- terity would have the benefit of. If all the committees of the Corporation were to act on the same lines the rates would be at 203. in the £. It was time they had an ex- planation. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Horeasesoie said he thought it was time that the revenue from the gas works went to relieve the rates. Owing to the extension of the borough an enor- mous amount of money was required to carry out all the necessary improvements. Councillor H. ROBERTS remarked that as the Gas Com- mittee practically accepted the position indicated by his resolution it relieved him of a goo 4 deal of responsibility and made it unnecessary for him to say much in reply. He thought that at the outset he had avoided anything in the nature of an attack upon the ck,mmittee. He had brought forward that resolution with only one object, and that was really to strengthen the backs at least of the majority of the members, who desired that the Gas Works should take their proper position as a financial concern, making a huge profit in connection with the

Corporation. He thought the res-,o:ation would bring that position about. He vroald have lil(Prl the ex-Mayor to have said something a little more defi,rite as to the future policy of the committee but he took it for granted at the moment at any rate that it was thnir i,,tfmtion that the present conditicn of thinzs, which h so Img,should cease,and that th- h Tough z,lio o'd receive the advantage of the profit made by t'i. ton iertakin. He tried to treat this matter seriously, en I he thought everyone of his friends aid,except Alderman Bolton. It seemed as if he forgot sometimes that he was en alder- man of the borough, and forgot the importance of the subject with which he was dealing. He never made the slightest reference to any serious statements made in his (Councillor Roberts') remarks. He said that some people could manage other people's affairs better than the peeple responsible. He further said he knew nothing at all about these figures and therefore could not be held responsible for them. It was not a very meditable admission fora member of the Gas Committee to make—first that other people could manage their business better than the people responsible, nor when he publicly admitted knowing nothing about the figures.

Alderman BOLTON : I rise to a point of order. I did not understand his figures. He does net understand them himself. (Laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said the alderman had misun- derstood him again. He said the Alderman knew noth- ing about the figured, and as a member of the Gas Com- mittee he ought te be ashamed to make any such admission. He was responsible along with the other nine members of the committee for those figures, and he ought to know something about them. If he did not it was time that he learned. The matter was of great im- portance and from a financial standpoint he did net think the Council had bad anything so serious before them for many years. They were at the parting of the ways, and if they did not divert from the policy that had obtained for many years, and apply themselves to the application of the profits made by gas manufacture to the relief of the rates there was no telling what the rates would become in the next few years. He believed the Gas Committee intended taking that course, and the resolution, if adopted, would strengthen their hands in the administration of the undertaking. The MAYOR said he thought a lot of good would arise out of the discussion, which had been carried on in a very temperate spirit. He might say that the course they had hitherto pursued had been approved of by the Local Government Board, but still they had taken a bit more out of revenue than they ought to have done. It was a safe course to follow but he did not think they would pursue it.

Aldeiman Fatactotron said that all he had to say for his own part and he knew the views et the Gas Conintit• tee, was that for the future the Gas Committee would spend no more money out of the revenue than they were entitled to. (Hear, hear.) Any m7ney that they wanted for the future they would come before the Council with plans for their sanction. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then carried.

div.head: CORPORATION OFFICIALS AND OUTSIDE DUTIES.
div.p: CORPORATION OFFICIALS AND OUTSIDE DUTIES.

In accordance with notice of motion given,Councillor Gluon moved "That Standing (",der No. 43 be amended by the omission of the words' or of the com- mittee by whom he was in the first place appointed.'." The order at present reads : "That no officer or servant of the Corporation,required by the terms of his appoint- ment to devote the wnole of his time to the duties of his offize, snail either directly or indirectly, by himself or any person, carry on or be engaged in any profession, trade, or business of any kind whatever, other than the profession, trade, or business of his office, without the sanction of the Council or of the committee by whom he was in the first place appointed." He said the Standing Order No. 43, which he moved a few months ago had been most loyally obeyed by the servants of the Corporation with the exception of two which he had in his mind. When the Standing Order was passed he quite expected that if any of the committees allowea Corporation employoe to undertake duties outsida their work for the Corporation, the com- mittee would follow the usual procedure and bring it before the Council for confirmation. In the particular cases he had in mind that procedure was not folio wed,and the consequence was that several members of the Council did not know that certain officials were working outside the Standing Orders. le should like to make it perfectly clear that he was not actuated by any feelings of hostility to any official of the Cerporation,but desired to place them on a higher plane than mere overtime seekers. The principle of the Standing Order was a good one, and would undoubtedly bring about a better state of affairs with respect to the servants of the Corporation. The Corporation should have the whole of their time and energies at their disposal. He contended that - a Corporation official who was occupied by business duties outside his own work, was not able to devote to the business of the Corporation that attention and business-like capacity which the Corporation had a right to expect for the money paid. There were other reasons why the Standing Order should be adhered to. It was distinctly unfair to professional men that they should be subjected to unfair competition on the part of Corporation servants. If a Corporation servant were in the running for outside employment, the inference was that he would get it because his position was a guaran- tee of his ability. Councillor H. ROBIIRTS seconded the resolution. He said the Standing Order as it now stood left it open for a committee to grant permission to a servant to take tip outside duties. Some committees were acting loyally to the intended spirit of the order and refusing te allow s3rvants to do so whilst other committees were giving permission. The result would be to set up a condition of jealousy between committees and officials. On the general question he thought that so far as the higher paid officials were concerned,they were paid sufficiently well to enable the Corporation to have the first call upon their ordinary time. He saw no reason whatever why these servants of the Corporation should seek other employment and deprive others of it. The Tows; CLERK said the Standing Order had no reference to the chief officials of the Corporation. They were pi ohited from taking outside work by the terms of their appointment.

Councillor ROBERTS said he used the word higher paid officials. He knew the chief officials were debarred from undertakiag outside work, but there were others who were getting salaries of £2OO and rnore,and the Corpora- tion had a right to expect that the same conditions should obtain with regard to them. Councillor PIERPOINT said he only knew one official of the Corporation who undertook outside duties, and if there was another he would like to know his name. He was aware that Mr. Howard of the Gas Department was carrying on the duties of sub-registrar for a district of Warrington. When the Gas Committee gave him per- mission he assured the committee that if he lost a couple of hours by this outside work he made it up the same day. Councillor SHAW GREEN explained the course taken by the Markets Committee when a servant applied for per- mission that his wife might undertake the duties of postmistress at Latchford. The committee acted in the spirit of the Standing Order, and declined to allow the application. Councillor WOODS said he could fully bear out what had been said by the Provious speaker. Every person employed by the Corporation ought to be an well paid that he need not desire to supplement his income by out- side work. .
Councillor GELCE said the Gas Committee said their officials had not time to prepare the report asked for, yet one of the officials could go outside and du extra work. . _
..,.... The motion was then carried. COUNCILLOR SHAW GREEN ASKS FOR ASSIS- TANCE FROM THE GAS COMMITTEE.

-- -- As the Council were rising. Councillor Shaw Green asked if there was any probability of the Gas Committee giving an explanation at an early date—____ Alderman BOLTON It IEI not on the minutes. (Cries of " Chair, chair.") Councillor Strew GREEN was eventually given leive to proceed. Be said be wanted an expression from tie Council as to whether the Council should give them something out of the rates in view of the fact that the year would close in a fortnight, and they would be pre- paring the estimates for 1898-9. The Gas Committee had made a profit during the past year,and be wished to know if they intended to make a grant to the Corpora- tion. . . _
Councillor Trxerfox : I think that Councillor Shaw Green should not come here at the last minute and ask us for an expression of opinion. Ho wants to tie the hands of the Gas Committee.

Alderraan Fera-cau—on—thoug'it it was hard lines to ask the gas consumers to bear the brunt of all this, while the ratepayers who did not consume the gas should have the profits. The MAYOR It is Out of order.
COUnCiliOr SHILLCOCK : The ratepayers had to lind the .money for tne Gas Works.
The Cou.ncil then rose.

div.head: OUR LOCAL-CHURCRES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL-CHURCRES.
WYCLIFFE P. S. k, SOCIETY.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Sunday,and the sixth year promises to be as Successful as its predecessors in point of attendance. Mr. Arthur Birch,of Great Sankey presided, and in the course of at, interesting address he referred to the Creation,and spoke of the dignified position of man. Proceeding to iefer to the clashing and warring of men's souls, he stated that in his opinion there were two great contending forces..... the forces of good and the forces of evil—and it behoved every man who knew his weakest points to fortify him- self against the enemy.—The address for the afternoon was delivered by Mr. Sharpe,of Manchester, who spoke upon" Religious education in elementary schools." Ha gave his experience as headmaster in a Manchester Board School,giving an example of how a bible lesson ought to be given. An organ solo was brilliantly executed by Mr. W. H. Payton. The service was also taken part in by Mr. Thomas Wallington and Mr. Robins.
The late Mr. Woolf Joel's assessable property in Eng- land is expected to rank above £1,500,000 for death dues.

div.p: LO.G.T. No. I CONVENTION, S.W. LaNCAslalli. The monthly meeting of the above was held it the Central Hall, George-street, St. Helens on Satur- day. Bro. Roberts, C.C.T. presided over a fair at- tendance of representatives from Warrington, St. Helens, Earlestown, Ashton, Wigan, Widnes, Leigh, and Tyldeeley. After the appointment of the vari. ous committees the Convention Secretary gave hie monthly report, showing a slight increase in the Convention area. The Executive Committee re- ported the prospects of opening new lodges at Go!- borne, Bryn, and Tyldesley. It was decided to hold the next session at Leigh, and to meet on the third Saturday in lieu of the second, in consequence of the Grand Lodge session in Easter week. Bro Roberts, D. Co., COT., gave a stirring address urg- ing the members to more active work. After the- usual votes of thanks the meeting terminated in the usual way.

It is said that the force of militia hich will take part in the manoeuvres on Salisbury Plain will include sevs rat Lancashire battalions. P. is probable that other Northern battalion' will be associated with them, and all the battalions which take part in the operations will have their period of training extended by seven days.
Official intimation has been given that the Order transferring Haydock frcm Warrington to the St. Helmut County Court district has been passed.
