SiTußesdriaßyNitart tßnEesgrEipme"olddieadge on e• Sir Henry lliftehirsooungeh oi it Bessemer. the romances of e -fivßigrhi ttiyshiLyuesatresy..H is he displayed the genius of the inventor and the indomitable perseverance of the pioneer in busi- ness. Many inventors have reaped few of the rewards of their exceptional ability, but this can not be said of BESSEMER. He was a many- sided man. He possessed not only the intellect and imagination which are necessary to conceive and design, but also the practical constructive ability of the great manufacturer. Sir HENRI- BESSEMER was the son of a French refugee, and was born at Charlton, Herts, at the beginning of 1813. His inventive faculties seem to have been, to a large extent, hereditary. His father was an ingenious eneehainciau, and the profitable type- founding business in which he was engaged when the future discoverer of the Bessemer "process " first saw the light, was conducted according to methods of his own contrivance. The young Bas- semen's talent was recognised and encouraged by the enlightened parent, who provided tools for his son's instruction and amusensmet. It may be said that BESSEMER'S business life began when h 3 was eighteen years of age, for at that time we find him engaged as an engineer in London. Then, as all through his later life, the busy inventive brain was always at work. His first notable contrivance appears to have been a stamp which could not be imitated or forged, an improvement which must have been greatly neededif it be true that the revenue authorities in those days lost about one hundred thousand pounds a year through the fradulent imitations of government stamps. The inventor's experience in connection with this stamp was a warning for him during the rest of his life. He offered it to the Stamp Office and he was promised that, if it were adopted, he should be rewarded with a super- intendency of stamps worth £5OO or £6OO a year. Ws a matter of fact, however, though the stamp 4, was adopted by the Government the young inven— tor never received any recompense. A few years later government bureaucrats again distinguished themselves in the usual way in connection with one of BESSEMER:3 inventions. In this case it was the design of a new gun, which was rejected by the officials of the British War Office without even a trial. 1t met with a different reception in France, and the trials which were made at Vincennes were of a satisfactory charac ter. The notable thing about this particular in— vention is,however, the fact that it put BmssEmEn, on the track, so to speak, of his great discovery in regard to the production of steel which very quickly revolutionised the iron trade of the world. A well-known French offieer,Commandant who was himself the inventor of a new rifle, re- marked to BESSEMER, after the eXperiments re- ferred to, that what was wauted was a stronger and tougher material than the metal then in use for the construction of artillery. This off-hand remark was a little grain of seed that fell upon fertile ground. BESSEMER seems to have at once grasped the full significance of the French officer's idea. He knew, it is said, at that time practically nothing of metallurgy so far as iron is concerned. Sheffield held a monopoly of the steel trade, and steel was only made there in small quantities and by such crude and laborious pro- cesses that it cost from £5O to £7O a ton. But the inventor's mind had been turned in the direction in which it was to accomplish its most fruitful work. After many expensive ex periments had been carried through with charac- teristic energy and pertinacity,BEssrmEn. at length discovered his famous method of steel-making. As one biographer says "far Huntsman's tiny pot containing 301bs. of metal, picked cut of the furn- ace with a pair of tongs, BESSEMER prov.:ded the converter which holds several tons of molten pig- iron according to size. For a slow and expe nsiva method, including hours, of " bakiug," BESSEMER substituted a process lasting less than half an hour, as picturesque as it is rapid and offective,for those who have witnessed a steel " blow " are not likely to forget it,'' But the new process was not at once received. with general favour. There were, as usual, unexpected difficulties ahead. The new method of steel-making did all that was claimed for it with the particular kind of pig-iron which BESSEMER had used in his own experiments, but it was afterwards found that iron centaining- -more phosphorus was not .so amenable' to mani- pulation. This was a eeriotie set-back. The word " failure " was, however, not to be found in BESSIEMT R'S dictionary. Ho at once began to devise meaes for dealing with the phosphoric impurities, and after about three more years of experimentatioa ha was in a position to claim tint ho could turn oat steel at £6 a ton- He now found, however, that the iron, masters of the country were in an extremely scep;ical frame of mind, and 1m Ti )13 0: I,ll'l woui Lip; the , num, was pr3ee3s after ne previous fui. are, P/E3SE
I
to re 13. )f 3. le Fee

compelled, in conjunction with a partner, to start troika of his own at Sheffield. The object-lesson Which he was able to give at these works was decisive. The price of bteel fell rapidly, and other iron manufacturers were compelled to adopt the new process. This was BESSEMER'S great work, and he was rewarded with wealth and honours. He derived an immense income from this inven- tion, and royal and other distinctions were con- ferred upon him. The name of Bcssam an is now a household word wherever there are workers in iron, and it will take a high place amongst the names of those who have advanced human knowledge and improved the lot of mankind.

IN an address to his constituents of A Danger to peace, Northampton on Wednesday, Mr. LABOUCHERE made some pointed and timely remarks with reference to the talk of war which now seems to be the fashion in certain quarters, and to the part as a war minister which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN evidently thinks himself des- tined to play. There can be no doubt that some of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S methods of con- ducting the business of the Colonial Office are a real danger to peace. It may be, as Mr. LABOITCRERE sarcastically suggests, that his success in bullying, too weak-kneed

Liberal Unionists of Birmingham has led him to the conclusion that it is 4esirable to adopt the flame policy towards foreign statesmen. As a matter of fact, Mr. CI:IA:WM aLAIN is displaying all the worst qualities of the pervert. II has not only renounced his old opinions but he rushes to

extremes in adopting the opinions of the party he has joined. Mr. LABOIICHERE declares that Mr. CRAMBERLAIN'S object is really to depose Lord gemsnußY from the Tory leadership by taking a Stronger and more violent line in foreign policy than the older statesman approves of. If that be 80, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is a m 1.3.1 who now needs very close watching.

The Board of Guardians election has not yet 4Pparently, excited emy large amount of public interest. It would be a pity. however ,if this Opportunity is allowed to pass without a fuller Ventilation of the questions of public-house assess- tents. That subject is attracting a great deal of attention in various parts of the country,and We know that the articles dealing with it which have appeared from time to time in the

"Examiner " have been followed very closely in several qaarters. This week we give in another column some more very suggestive figures. It i 8 Contended by the apologists of the Assessment Committee,that public-houses should not be assessed according to the extraordinary prices paid for the houses at auction sales, but upon a fair rental. But are Warrington public-houses at present assessed upen a fair rental? For if that be so, how does it Come that as soon as the Corporation acquires two Public-houses and submits the tenancy to open Competition the rents and,of course,the assessments as well, are doubled and even trebled ? This is a

very important matter from a ratepayers point of view, for when public houses are under-assessed other property is over-assessed in comparison. It lE an extraordinary anomaly amounting even to a Public scandal, if public housas which are tied to brewers are assessed on a lower scale than those houses which belong to a public body like the Cor- poration. This is a qaestion which will have to be laced openly and candidly, and there is no better

opportunity than the present,when members of the Board of Guardians are seeking re-election. If we alight make a suggestion it would be that Mr. Pilling, who is the Chairman of the Board of Guardians and the Assessment Committee, should deal with the matter either at a public meeting or in some other way, for the benefit of his constituents and of the town generally.

The case which was concluded at the Warrington %tufty Court last Thursday occupied four sittings, alid was therefore one of the longest that has been Ileard in Warrington. The more one sees of these 48,38 the more one is forced to conclude that it ras high time the law relating to employers' lia- 41itY was simplified and improved generally, in the /ierests both of the emplcyer and the workman. lo e labour, anxiety, and cost of pro- blußed litigaton of this character, in ' thanY cases, inflict great hardship upon I'? parties chiefly concerned. Mr. Chamber- lain claims that his new Workmen's Compensation ACt, which will come into force at the beginning of JUly this year, will not be a "lawyers employ- relent "Act, but a genuine contrivance for securing ,compensation for injuries. But working men have neard promises of that kind with regard to other legislathe measures, and the promises have not al- Ways been fulfilled.

div.head: CLOSING OF THE "CARRIAGE DRIVE," HELSBY.
div.p: THE CLOSING OF THE "CARRIAGE DRIVE," HELSBY.

At the Runcorn Rural District Council meeting on Tuesday,at Dutton,the Clerk to the County Council (ar, a. Potts) wrote stating that the Helsby Parish Council had petitioned under 28 (4) of Local Govern-. Ment Act 1894, that a public footpath within the oarip and known as the" Carriage Drive," leading from the, Chester main road over Helsby Hill had been recently stopped up by a tenant of the Marquis of Cholmondeley with the knowledge and consent of his lordship's agent, and such petition states that the District Council upon reProsentation made to them had failed to take proceed- Lliga in the matter. He (Mr. Peas) purposed submitting the Petition to the Local Government Acts Committee of the County Council at its next meeting,and in the mean- time he would be glad to be favoured with the observa- tions ol the Rural District Council thereon. The Cleik said the road was made by the Marquis of Cbolmondeley more than 27 years ago over the hill across his own land and it came out on the Chester-road, The Helsby Parish Council passed a resolution miring tbe Rural Council to take preceedings to prevent the Mar- quis from stopping up the road. They (the Council) referred the matter to him, and he had come to the con- clusion that the Marquis of Cholmendeley was quite iustified in closing the road. The Helsby Parish Council were not satisfied, and they went to the Chester County eotlnei I. Mr. Baxter asked whether there was any road before the Marquis made the present one. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL GUILD. At the weekly meeting of the above society on Wed- nesday evening,Mr. G. A. Hayes read a paper on "The spirit of fun in literature." There was a large attend- ance' and the paper proved most interesting. A discus- sion followed. SLEEPING IN IRE SALT WORKS. At the Runcorn Police Court on Friday, before Messrs. A. .R. Norman and W. Timmins, Edgar Hatton, of Middlewich. was charged ve.th sleeping on the premises of the Silt Works, that morning. P.C. Bancroft proved the case.—Superintendent Okell said Hatton was a very good workman when steady. He appeared to have given way to drink. Prisoner promised to mend his ways,and he was discharged. " THE IRISH BRIGADE."

The above was the title eta lecture delivered en Mon- day evening in St. Edward's chools,Mill Brow,Runcorn, by the Rev. Father Stanley of St. Mary's, Latchford, Warrington. The lecture was illustrated with lime light views,the lantern being manipulated by Mr. T. Bowyer. Views of the different places which the brigade marched through were shown on the screen, and were explained in an admirable manner by the rev, lecturer who ap- peared to he master of his subject.

LECTURE ON ST. PATRICK. On Sunday evening, immediately after the evening service, the members of the St. Edwards League of the Cross Society, assembled in the L ‘ague Hall, for the purpose of hearing a lecture on the if fe of St. Patrick, patron saint of Ireland. Mr. Clynch, of Rock Ferry.and an ex-president of the Runcorn Society, delivered a lecture, which proved most interesting. The usual votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN. . The usual weekly concert was given in the above institute on Tueiday evening. There was a fair attendance and the programme was gone through in an admirable manner. Miss Warburton, Mr. J. W. Williams, and Mr. R. Jardine, entertained the company, by giving songs 863. The audience appeared to appreciate the efforts of the artistes. Toe concert c:used with toe customary votes of thanks being passed. A NEGLECTFUL HUSBAND AT RUNCORN. At the Runcorn PoliB Court on Friday morning be- fore Mr. A. R. Norman (in the chair) and Mr. W. Tim mins, Edward Ivens, boatman, was charged out remand with neglecting to contribute towards his maintenance. It was explained that his wife, Jane Ivens,got an order from the magistrates in July 1896 against her husband for 7s. 6.1. for her maintenance under the Married Womens Act. The arrears amounted to £5 Ba. 6.1. guilty and promised to Pap £2 in court aPnridsotirer pleaded der in instalments.—Mrs. Ivens agreed to this and the prisoner was discharged. BETHESDA P.S.A.

The usual weekly meeting of the above society MO held on Sunday afternoon, in the Bethesda Congrega- tional Church, RUDOO[D, Mr. W.Handley presiding. The speaker was Mr. Hooper, a Meth° list Free Church evangelist, who, taking Joshua for his model, gave a stirring address on the strengt h of charactn and por- pose. The soloists were Miss Withington, who sang effectively " Eternal City," and Miss Isiira Handley, of Garston,who recited "The Land of Gold." The speaker and soloists had a very hearty reception from the crowded meeting. The Secretary announced that the open meeting would bt held that day fortnight. The monthly meeting or the above committee was held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall, Mr. D. Bis- brown presiding. 'Meru were also present Messrs. Handley, CunninghamAßiley,Sweetman, Hankinson, J. Pritchard, J. D. Jones (librarian and secretary), and J. Wilding (surveyor) The librarian presented his report as follows :—Lendin. department : Theology 18, phil• osophy 11, science 75', history 117, poetry 19, fiction 1587, miscellaneous 205, music 19, total 2,029, decrease on the corresponding month of last year 10. Reference depart- ment: miscellaneous 53,increase on corresponding month of last year 9. The report was adopted. The Chairman was cordially thanked ti e his services during the year, on the motion of Mr. Cunningham, seconded by Mr. Hankinson. The Chairman suitably responded. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—AN ALLEGED lIIREGULASITY.

Mr. J. E. Worsley held an inquiry on Thursday morn! lug at the Police Court, into the circumstances attend- ing the death of James Lydian, the nine weeks old child of Clara and John Lydia% who died on Saturday, the 12th inst.—The mother of the child said they bad been living in Salford up to a fortnight ago. At present she lived in Bridgewater-st. with her mother. The deceased had been very delicate since birth. Witness took the child the week previous to the 4th March to Dr. Wray Strange, of Salford. The doctor treated it ior whooping cough. The child died on Saturday lait. No doctor saw it in Runcorn. Witness wrote to her husband who is working in Salford as a dock labourer to get a certifi- cate of death from Dr. Wray Strange and he did, The certificate produced was the one she recsived.—The Coroner said this was a question of alleged irregularity. It appeared that a certificate had been given for the death, and he intended therefore to adjourn the enquiry for the purpose of obtaining evidence from a person who saw the doctor in Salford, and obtained from him a certifleate about which this euquiri was mainly being held. The inquiry was adjourned for a week. ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN CONsrABM, At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, the magis- trates present being Mr. G. L. Davies (chairman), and Mr. R. A. Norman,two persons from Warrington named William Ross and Annie Ross, were charged with as- saulting P.O.Gregory whilst in the execution of his duty in Viear-street. Runcorn, on Saturday night, and also with using obscene language at the same time and place. The constable stated that at 11.45 on Saturday night he was on duty in High-street,when he heard a disturbance in Vicar-street. He proceeded there and saw prisoner at Mrs. Farrell's lodging-house. They were quarrelling and creating a disturbance. The male prisoner threw a lamp at his wife and broke it. He asked witness what he wanted there,and he told him he was a police officer. Ross darted at him, knocked him down, rushed into the house and fastened the door. Mrs. Farrell opened the door and witness went in. The prisoners rushed at him and knocked him into the yard. He sent for assistance and P.C. Bowyer arrived on the scene. They got in the house and proceeded to take Ross into custody. The female prisoner then became very violent and tore wit- ness's coat off his back and kicked him. She was en- deavouting to free her husband. The male prisoner be- haved like a madman, and they had to handcuff him before they could get him to come to the police station. The language of prisoners was dispaceful.—P.C.Bowyer gave confirmatory evidence.—The Chairman remarked that prisoners had a very bad record. For the assault they would be committed to Hnutsford Gaol for one month each with hard labour and for the second offence 14 days' hard labour each. EXTENSION OF THE LIBRARY—LOCAL GOVIIRNAIRST
BOARD INQUIRY.

Oa Wednesday morning. Colonel Leurd, WE., held an inquiry in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, Runcorn, into the application of the Runcorn Urban District Council, for sanction to borrow £250 and to appropriate certain land for the purpose of extending the Free Library. There were present the following members of the Free Library Committee :—Messrs. D. Bisbrown (chairman), W. Handley, J. Pritchard, and J. D. Jones, (librarian and secretary), with F. A. Lake (law clerk), and J. Wilding (surveyor). Mr. Wilding produced the plan and explained that it was intended to use up certain land which was now vacant for the purpose of making a general reading room, and to convert the site occupied by the astmit and coal place into an entranc, hall. It was also intended to convert the old reading room into a book store-room and refer- ence library. The entrance would be in Egerton-street, and a visitor immediately on passing the doorway would be in a place which would lead into a central hall. A ladies' room would be on the left and a general reading room straight in front. The hall would be lighted by means of a skylight and light from the general reading room by means of glazed screens. The general reading room wouln be lir•hted by a window occupying t.,.(3 whole of the north end,and also by a series of windows 261 t long and 61t high on the east side, to be opened by means of a swivil in order to get an air wash. The place would be thoroughly ventilated. The usual conveniences would be provided.—The in- spector pointed out that the money would probably be lent for 30 years, and the annual repayment would be .£l2. He inquired how it was proposed to pay this money.—Mr. Lake replied that the Free Library Com- mittee rented the present premises from the UrJan District Couccil and the annual cost of the proposed extension would be added to their rent.—The Inspector then made an examination of the present premises and the site of the proposed addition.

Sr. PAUL'S MIN'S BIBLB CLASS.

At the weekly meeting of the above society on Sunday afternoon, Mr. R. H. Posnett gave an address on"Dey." Mr. B. Crosby sang in a pleasing manner, and Mr. Bowyer gave a selection on the organ. A FALL Dows QUARRY.

On Saturdav'afternoon a serious accident happened to a lad named iintaiol Haugh,aged eight years,living with his parents at 8, Curzon-street, Runcorn. Tne lad was flying a kite on Runcorn Hill when he fell down the dis- used quarry, a distance ot about 30 feet. His fall was fortunately hra'aen by his alighting on a ledge or the consequences would have been much more s,,rious. He sustained terrible injuries about the head. He was taken home,and Dr. Ormsby was called in. The lad is now progressing very favourably towards recovery. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

As a lurry belonging to the Co-operative Society was being driven down Penketh-lane, into High-street, on Friday, a lad named Hayes, who had jumped on the back part of the vehicle for the purpose of having a ride, got one of his feet fast between , the spokes of the back wheel. The driver, although • not aware of the dancrons position that Hayes was in, pulled up im- mediately for the purpose of making a call. Had not the driver pulled up at that point the toy's foot would have gone round with the wheel and must hAvd been wrenched off. So fast was the foot wedged between the spokes of the wheel that it was found necessary to cut away a portion of the wood before the lad could be re- leased. His foot was badly crushed, but fortunately no boars were broken. He was taken to his home in Nelson- btreet, and attended to by a doctor.

div.head: BICYCLE ACCIDENT AT RIINC3RN,
div.p: BICYCLE ACCIDENT AT RIINC3RN,

About eleven o'clock on Saturday night, an accidrnt befel Mr. Samuel Webster, cycle agent of Lowland-road, Runcorn, in Halton-road, as he was returning home from Warrington after the football match at that town. On Saturday night rain led rathor heavily and made the roads very slippery. Mr. ‘Vebster Was accompanied by three other wheQlmen and when war the Graws Inn, Halton-road, his machine skidded and threw its rider into the road. His companions were in fren*, and on hearing the noise they returned, and found Mr. Webster lying unconscious in the roadway. They carried him to a neighbouring house, and afterwards conveyed him home. The next morning Dr. Delaney was called in, and under the latter's care he is progressing favourably towards recce:Ty. Mr. Webster sustained very serinus injuries about the head. FUNERAL OF Miss JENNIE ISHERWOOD, RUNCORN. The funeral of alms Jennie Isherwood, aged 36 years, whose death took place on Sunday, at Lynwood Howe, Norman-road (the ro,sidencr, of her sister, Mrs. Isaac Stubbs) took place on Wednesday afternoon, in the Run- corn Cemetery. The deceased lady Wag well ltown in Runce.rn, and her death will occasion regret among a large circle of friends. She contracted a chill about 12 months ago,and pulmonary complications ensued, and despite all medical science and devoted nursing could do, she fell a victim to consumption,and pass, d away on Sunday. The following attended the funeral:—Mr Lewis, Mr. and Mrs. Aehworth (Northwich),Mr.W.Smith ver- pool). Mr. Leanard Stubbs, Mrs.Per&val, and Mrs. Guy. The carriers were, Messrs. J. Hughes, L M ,rris,W.Carr, W. Worrall, W. Hulse, and W. Elgar. There were also present the Rev. S. Wright, the Rev, R. Percival,Messts. S. Cooker, J. Clarke, T. Parry, Guy, Scragg, Gandy, J. Newall,Jones, Moores, J. Newall,jun , Holferd, W. New- all,W.Cooke, H. Wright, and W. Gandy. At the grave- side the people assembled, sang the hymn " Jesus Lover of my Soul." The Revs. S. Wright and R. Perc:val pre- formed the burial service. Wreaths were sent by the following :—Mr.and Mrs. Aahworth, Mr. F.Lewis, Mr.and Mrs. Le Galliene,Mr. and Mrs. Harry Wright, employe, and Mrs.Yarwead(Frodsham). It was stated oy a married woman named Taylor,with whom the deceased and his wife and two children had recently !edged, that he did not appear to be unkind to his wife, but they had not lived happily together. On Thursday Mrs. Rushton left home, presumably to go to work,but did not return. On Saturday her husband received an unstamped letter from her stating that she did net intend to return to him, preferring to work and keep herself and one child if he would maintain the other. She ,omplainel that he spoke to her and treated her "like a dog," and it was a pity that they had married so soon. It could. " only be a liking, not love " which he showed towards her when he married hut.. This letter greatly ii peat the deceased. On Saturday afternoon he returned to his work at the L. and Y. Railway Carriage works, Newton Heatb,and later ia the day his dal body was found in a tank, close to which were found the deceased's cap, muffler and waistcoat. The jury found that the deceased had committed suicide whilst insane —Deceased was buried in the Rine C tery on Thursday after- noon.

div.head: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.-CONCERT LAST NIGHT.
div.p: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.-CONCERT LAST NIGHT.

St. Patrick's day was celebrated this year at Itu'morn in the usual fashion. The shamrock and green ribbon emblems were gaily worn by most of Ireland's sons and daughters. In the evening a concert was held in the Public Hall there being a very fair attendance. The first item on the programme was a march by the Wi nei Peze Subscription Band. A duet "The Sail's Sighs," was well rendered by Miss Shokin and Mr. M.rria. Mr. I F. Shingler received the plaudits of the audience f'r his rendition of " The Bugler," whilst Miss Milne of Prod- sham, and her pupil., the Misses Id. Allen, Atkinson,and Csrlisle (2) for their selection on mandolines were en- cerel. Song, " Ora Pro Noble" was rendered very effectively by Mr. Wesley Cooke. Mr. Ciaddock, accompanied on the piano by hi wife, gsve a piccolo solo. "On the March,"a comic song, rendered by Mr. J. Taylor, highly pleased the audience, and he was given an encore. He sang " Too strong, too strong." This proved equally amusing and kept the audience in uncontrollable laugh or for several minutes. For her rendition of " The Miller and the Maid," Miss A. WITSII3 was well received. Mr. A. Shingler gave " The Village Blacksmith," (The VS idnes Eisteddfod priz song) in fine style. A euphonium solo was given by Mr. T. Hynes "I'm not particular," and a comic song. by Mr. J. Taylor brought forth a laud outburst of applau,e, and at the close of the song he was again called upon. He re- plied with another "comic" which Visaged his hearers im- mensely. Other items were---song,Mr. T. Johnson ; "The Diver," Mr. F. Shingler; seleetioa (rnancelines) Miss Milne s Cereza Band; song, "Thy voice is m ar me," Mr. Cooketselectioes by the band ,"Ls favourite""hAacteth," and "Gems of Victorian Melody." Miss Dukes proved an efficient accompanist. At the interval the Ray. Father Gore appeared before the audience, and thanked them for their support. Be also thanked the artistes who had come from Warrington. Widnes, and Frudsham,and also their local artistes. Immediately atter the concert, a "dance" was held, there being a fair attendance. An excellent programme of dances was submitted, and this was gone through without the slightest hitch.

div.head: THEFTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THEFTS AT RUNCORN.
PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Before Mr. Walter Timmins, and Mr. A. R. Norman, at the Runcorn Police Court on Friday, Carl Leyon, a Norwegian sailor,was charged with Healing an autoharp, value 12s. 6, the property of Ada Churchill, on the 15th January. and also with stealiug a pair of boots from the shop of Arnold Unsworth, Percival-lane, Runcorn. After evidence had been given the Chairman said they were satisfied that the prisoner was guilty of the charges, but they took into consideration the fact that he had only just come out of prison after serving six weeks in gaol, and they would only commit him for 10 days hard labour on each charge. At the same Court, John Richard Marshall, a respect- able looking man, was charged on remand with stealing on the 3rd March is. 6d. by means of a trick from John Me.Malion at Weston Point.—The prosecwor said he was a clerk and lived at 904 Stockport-road, Le venshulme, Manchester. On Thursday, the 3rd inst. he came to Runcorn. He met prisoner in the Mariners' Hotel, Per- cival Lane, Runcorn. Prisoner told him that he had been engaged on a ship which was lying at Saltport. as a steward and cook. Witness and prisoner walked down to Weston Point where he had business. They pasted and Marshall afterwards called at the shop where he was and showed him a paper signed " Swinton," who he said was the captain of the Norwegian vessel on which he had yet employment. He asked for scene money promising him that he would give it him back at eight o'clock that evening. Prisoner promised to bring witness a parrot. He also promised the landlord of the Mariners' Arms one. Witness lent him the money on the promise that he would pay it back.—John Peter Sjoblad, a Russian Finn, of the vessel "Cashier "lying at Salt- o )rt, said prisoner ha I never been engaged to serve on his vessel. He had never sailed with her. Their cap- tain's name was Furgusen.—Marshall was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour. Thomas Trelfer, residing. at Wivern-place, Runcorn. , was charged on remand with stealing 50 fathoms of rope. value £1 93., the property of Joseph Sh4llcross,on the 3rd March.—Mr. F. A. Lake, who appeared for the prisoner, said the CASO was one of mistaken identity. He should call the prisoner's felner and uncle, and they would tell the Bench that the prisoner was at home at seven o'clock on the 3rd inst.,snd that he was in bed by 7-30, and never got out of bed until ten o'clock on the following morning.—Tnomas Trelfer, father of the pri- soner,gave evidence in support of MeL ike's statement. In reply to Superinteadeut Okell,the witness said it was net true that the prisoner was at the Post Office at eight o'clock the same evening.—The mavatrates eventually remended the prisoner for another week,in order tosee if the police could find the rope.

CHILD NEGLECT AT WARRINOTON.—A LAZY FATHER SENT TO GAOL. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Friday morning before the Mayor, and Councillors Roberts and Smethurst, Frederick Cooper, 27, West-street. was charged with having on the 3rd March and during the past six menthe neglected five of his children, viz., Elizabeth, Frederick Thocnas,Harry, Stanley,and Annie. —lnspector McAteer prosecuted far the N.S.P.C.C. and said the defendant was the father of six children aged from 16 years to 5 years. The eldest girl was employed at the mill and earning 4s a week. In consequence of a complaint from defendant's wife be went to defend- ant's house on 3rd March and found defendant present with his children. Be examined the children and found them wearing only one garment and almost shoeleee. The soles were off their shoes. The home was badly furnished and the bed occupied by the family was badly off for covering. Defendant said he had been out of work for 5 or 6 weeks. His wife said in defendant's pres- ence4that he had been out of werk for 28 weeks and had given her only £2 to support herself and family. The wife had to go out washing and got between four and Ave shillings, out of which she had to pay 3s. 9d. for rent. On the Bth of March he went again and found de- fendant in the house muddled hi drink. The family had been supported by Mrs. Cooper's relatives and friends for the past six months. Defendant was a lazy man. There was a nephew living with them who paid 9s. a week for maintenance.—Mrs.Cooper said that defendant bad been out of work about 30 weeks and she had bad the six children to keep. Her husband had had work but had thrown it up. But for the kindness of her rela tivee and friends the children would have starved. De- fendant had had some work last Saturday and earned 4s. but he gave her none. He bad also pawned a counterpane and kept the money. During the past six months she had had £3 2s from defendant and when she told him he had been out of work for 29 weeks he said he would be out of work for 39 weeks and would not keen her. Defendant WAR not a sober man.—Mrs.Bloom- field, V. Lairs-stestated that defendant had never done his duty to his wife and children.—Defendant alleged as his excuse that his work at the forge had made him incompetent as a carpenter, and he could not get work. The Mayor said he was very sorry indeed for defendant's wife,and he had used her shamefullylle would be corn• mitted to prison for a month's hard labour.—Patrick and Catherine Ryan, Silver-it., appeared on a charge of neglectine two children.—This case Is-id been adjourned for a raonth.—lnspector McAteer said that though they kid removed from Pump-yard to Silver-st. there was no imnroveroent in the condition of the home and children. —Defendants pleaded earnestly for another chance,and after hearing the evidence the magistrates adjourned the case again for five weeks. WARRINGTON GIRLS SENT TO A. Et OMR. At the Warrington Bornueh Police Court, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr T. Birchen, two young girls, named Fanny Dalonze, 1, Milford-st., and Emily Jones, 4,Dudley-st.,were charged,the former with stealing articles of wearing apparel value 135., and the latter underclothing value 78.3d.,fr0m the workroom of Charles Bird,draper,in Bank-st..between the let January and the 10th inst.—Both girls pleaded guilty.—The Chisf Constable said this was a very painful ease. The prisoners were only nineteen and seventeen years old respectively, and they had been in Mr. Bird's employ for about twelve months. Mr. Bird was a draper,carrying on business at Padzate-lane, and also had a stall in the market. His workroom was in Bank-et., and he employed a number of girls, including the prisoners. Between January and the present time Mr. Bird strongly suspected that there had been robberies going on in the workroom, but be could not fix it upon any et the employes. He had occasion to go to Deleoze's house, and when there saw a dozen yards of expensive lace lying about, and he suspected that it was his property. He communicated with Detectives Mona- Os° and Forger, and they visited the house and found the articles. When Delooze was questioned she admitted baying stolen the articles, and incriminated Jones. The prisoners incriminated each other. Delooze had neither father nor mother, and lived with her sister. Jones had no mother and resided with her father. He had spoken to the girls but they had refused to go to a home.—Mr. Birchen It is a very sad case.—The Chairrran (to the prisoners) : It is a melancholy case, it makes my heart ache to see you starting a career of that kind.—Mr. Bir- chen You are on the way to ruin—we an see what your future will be.—The Chief Constable asked that the Case might be adjenrned a few minutes, m that Mr. Taylor, police court missionary, might speak to them with a view of getting them to go to a home. On the ease being called again, however, Mr. Taylor said the girls refused to accept the offer. Still the magistrates asked them to reconsider their decision, and after Mr. Talbot had spoken to them they gave an undertaking to go to a home for twelve months, and on .that under- standing a conviction only was recorded against them.

WARRINGTON v. RUNCORN.
A CLOSE GAME.

This return match was played off at Warrington on Saturday before 6,000 spectators a few hundred ot whom had come from Runcorn. The weather was bright and sunny,w!iile the field was in a condition not to be improved upon. In view of their big task at Oldham this Saturday the Cheshireme.n rested 1 Houghton, Robinson, and Nioort-s, while the only absentee on the home side was Ilorrison in the for- wards. sir. Priestley, of Broughton Rangers, was the referee, and the teams were composed as fol- lows:

Runcorn: Jolley,full back; Warder, Butterworth, Woods, and West, threequarters; Faulkner and Nixon, half-backa; Farmer, Langley, Walker,Gayter, Darlington, Lightfoot, Bettley, and Antrobus, for- wards.

Warrington : Boscow, full back; Moores, Isher- wood, Hallam, and Raynor, threequarters ; J. T. Bate and Duckworth, half-backs; Taylor. Deakin, Naylor, Fairhurst, Swift, Hill, Mason, and Hatton, forwards.

The homesters won tho toss and Farmer otarted far Runcorn against a slight breeze. Faulkner secured from the first scrimmage and handed to West who punted to B3SCOW, the home frill back returning promptly. A round of kicking between the respective sets of backs gave Warrington a alight advantage, but play settled at half way for a brief spell. Then Runcorn were penal- ieed and Hallam punted powerfully. Wends mulling and letting the homesters well into Cheshire quarters. The same player was at fault a minute later and Runcorn wero hard pressed. Isherwood marked cleverly and gave his side a fine position. Raynor broke sway but was chcek.od near the line, and then Smack Bate was seen following suit only to loole possession of the oval when nearly over. Warrington were getting posession frequently and Moores was also nearly a snorer from a pass by Bate. Faulkner punted and Raynor securing smartly dropped fruitlessly at goal. Even- tually West got the ball away and tackled Boscow the homesters being forced to defend. fsherwood,Moores, and Hallam returned to the attack, hut Butterworth made a grand mark on his own line. Play was fast and exciting. both ends of the rl being visited in turn. A neat round of passing by Faulkner, Botterworth and Warder looked bad for the home lot,but Boscow came to the rescue. A spirited dash by the home front rank was the reply to the effort, ani the next movement Moores was carried off hurt. Runcorn had no an advantage In the packs and gave the home defence some trouble. Butterworth rendered grand service to his aide, but while Runcorn were pressing, Hallam intercepted a pass and had a clear course but lack of speed lost him a try. Butterworth broke away cleverly but passed forward when near the borne line. A mast exciting tussle was witnessed in Warrington territory, Boscow relieving with a finelyledged kick teem touch. Moores hereabouts resumed amid cheers. H Allem had a shy at goal and lest ground by it. Woods fumbled again however, and Warrington were hot on the attack, Raynor stepping in the breach promntly when Boscow was miring up A mysterious decision against Warrington by the referee gave Runcorn the advantage and Isherwood carried the ball over in saving. Determined play on the line fol- lowed. Bate, Duckworth, Isherwood, and Moores raised the siege in a clever manner, half-ticne arriving with a blank sheet. Taylor started the final moiety and Warrington went off with a promising burst. Boscow centered under the posts, but Butterworth cleared, and then ran the home full-back in touch at centre. Grand passing by Faulkner and Warder would have lei to a try but for the later knocking on at the critical moment, Butterworth dropped at goal and failed, Deakin leading the Warring- ton forwards in a splendid dribble to centre. Duckworth smartly followed up and tackled Jolley. Warrington pressing warmly. Isherwood forced Jolley to kick in touch at the corner. 803C0V7 centred and Jolley failing to secure, Duckworth had the hardest of luck in not scoring. A penalty kick changed the venue, Butterworth also as- sisting with a prompt tackle of Isherwood.Deakin headed another rush which only temporarily relieved,Jolley and Butterworth returning with interest. Nixon and Butter- worth dodged through but were upset near the coveted line. A severe attack was maintained, and Raynor mull- ing badly Warrington had a very serious time. Play settled under the goal, and Faulkner passed back to Butterworth who dreoped a goal which had an element of doubt about it. The point was allowed, and though Warrington made strenuous efforts they were repelled ciontinuously and by Butterworth nearly every time. , Near the close a comhinad effort by Bate and Moore; raised Warrington's hopes, but the latter was plainly a sufferer from his iajury acid failed to get through the Cheshire defence. The game soon ended with Runcorn holding a lead of one goal (2 points) to Warrington nil.
AN ESSAY ON HEELS.i

Of all the places in the human body where we should or expect to find disease, the heel would naturally seem to head the list. The heel is built to stand on and to walk with; it is a hard, foundational thing. It is made to do a lot of work and endure no end of scraping and friction without giving any sign of sensibility. It is not a point of the body which is apt to "catch" things. It never comes to the front socially, as handsome fingers and noses do, and artists are not apt tar set any great store by it, A man may go through a whole lifetime and never have any trouble with his heel except it gets bruised or bitten by a snake or a vicious dog. Yet there is one complaint which attacks a man's heel, and, curi- ously enough, attacks it for the rery reason that /Mature has apparently thought so little of it as to furnish it with a very low aal slosv blood circulation. And, oh ! my friends, when there is anything serious the matter with that humble portion of our anatomy, how we are punished for the small esteem with which we have regarded it. A pedestrian with a crippled heel is, of course?, completely done, and even a bicyclist with a sore heal will leave his wire horse„in;the stable until his heels are as sound as his toes. -

- Now,pleasejet us hear what Mr. McGregor has to say about his experience with a sore heel, andlafterwards will tell you what, in my opinion, ailed it. "in March of 1895," he says, " my left heel became inflamed and painful. I could /scarcely hobble about and all day long I was in pain. I kept cn with my work with difficulty, but at night was quite worn out, and could hardly bear the pain. I went to a doctor, who recommended hot fornentations, but I got no relief. After months of suffering I read about Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup and Plasters. I applied one of the Plas- ters to the painful part, and as my system was in- flamed, I took Mother Seigel's Syrup according to the directions. I 8000 found great relief, and after continu- ing the treatment for a fortnight I was completely cured,and have not hied an ache or pain since that time. I have told many persons of the cure and you can pub- lish this statement as you think fit. Signed (S. McGre- gor, 111, Gallowgate. Aberdeen, July 6th, 1897.) , What was it ailed Mr. McGregor's heel and how did Mother Seigel's Syrup cure it ? If we are able to answer this it will be a very important point gained. For here was our friend practically incapacitated for months by severe pain in an unpretentious but exceedingly useful Pitt of his body. The great Achilles died of a wounded heel; but Mr.McGregor does not attribute his trouble to an Iniurv.lf he had been hurt he weuld have told us so, and the entire case would have been different. New,if you will kindly follow ms along while I talk a little while, perhaps we shall get some light on the subject ley means of an illustration or two. Fancy a brook or stream of some width running through meadowlaed. When the stream runs straight, and with sufficient descent to give it an impulse,it never gets clogged up. On the contrary, where the ground is almost level and the stream proceeds with many turns and twists, some of them quite abrupt, it is sure to de- posit in those corners much of the loose stuff,leaves and sticks, and such like, which float on its surface. Or when the stream is comparatively narrow you find the channel deeper and the water more rapid. Then again, when it spreads out broad the water is shallow and slow and tenth to form gravel or sand-bars in the middle, as you have often noticed. Now observe. To Woad is a stream circulating con- stantly through the body by moans of the arteries and veins. lodigestion or dyspepsia with torpid liver manu- factures and throws into the b!ood a substance called uric (toil. It is a very fine crystal, insnluble in water, hard as powdere I glass, and a virulent poison,—a very nasty and dangerous combination of qualities. It may set up id:tome:teflon anywhere, but is almost certain to do so wlsere the circulation is retarded and small in volume. The tips of the oars, the old scars of wounds, &c., and the hod are among these places. In plain Saxon the poison sticks in the heel and sets up an acute inflammation which we ctll gout. That was Mr. Mc- Gregor's malady. Mother Seigel's Syrup drove the piosen from his blood, righted his digestion, and set him on his legs again. Dear me, how simple and beautiful a puzzle is when you once come to understand it.

OallAghan corroborated and said he found a rabbit In the net which had been killed by a ferret.—Defendant arse fined 20s. and costs or a month's hard labour in default. CRUELTY TO A BOAT HORSE Charles LOWS, a yonth,was charged with working a horse In an unfit state at Burton- wood on February 21st, and Richard Price. the owner, was charged with causing it to be worked.—Both pleaded guilty, —lnspector Grentrex, R.S.P.C.A. said that on the day stated be WAS on the canal bank at Burtonwood when he saw Lowe In charge of two horses with a boat load of sand. The lead- ing horse was aged and had two wounds on the shoulder the size of a half crown and shilling respectively.—The Bench fined Price 10s. and eosts. and Lowe the costa only. SLEEPING OUT—Samuel Bradford. a disreputable looking tramp, was charged with sleeping "out in the open air, to wit ins hay stack," at Newton without visible means on March 16th,—The case was proved and the Chairman in sen- tencing prisoner to 14 days hard labour said he was one of a very dangerous class of people who were very often the cause of haystacks getting on fire. RUNCORN PET EY NESSIONS. Mom:wt.—Before Mr. G. L. Davies (in the chair), and Mr. A. R. Norman. TEMPORARY ATITHORITY.—James Tatlock was granted per- mission to sell at the Oddfellows' Arms, Wellington-street, Runcorn. Hog-PAYMENT or POOR RATE.—There were 76 summonses for the non-payment of this rate. A number of cases had been settled. but in the majority the usual order for pay ment was made. div.head: SOCIAL PROBLEMS.
div.p: SOCIAL PROBLEMS.
WAR AND FOOD SUPPLIES.
By JOSEPH HYDER, General Secretary of the. Land Natimalisapion Society.
ARTICLE XIX.

We have all read of the horrors of the siege of Paris. I ata thinking of the horrors of the siege of London. Six millions of people—multitudes of them ill-fed a th• best—uniting and waiting with growing anguish for the food from abroad that lies at that moment sunk beneath the seas by an enemy's war-ships. WILLIAM JAMESON (" Coming Fight with Famlne.") . . .

The air is filled with wars and rumours of ware. thin- powder is lying loose in all parts of the globe,and at any time it may be exploded. This is not the view of a mere alarmist. It is a fact that is patent to all the world. And it suggests some very serious reflections for thoughtful people. Not the least of these is the ques- tion, "How would England's prospects of success in a great war be affected by her increasing dependance upon other countries for her food supplies ? " Apart altogether from the enormous loss in other respects occasioned by ' our land going out of cultivation, there remains the danger to which we are exposed in the event of our country becoming involved in a life-and-daath struggle with some strong Power or Powers. With a population of nearly 40.000,000, we grow food for only about one- fourth of that number. and have to laving food for the other 30,000,000. It follows Etat, As all that food has to be brought across the sea from other lands, our national safety entirely depends upon our naval supremacy. If we were to lose the command of the Rea we ehould thus be speedily within measurable distance of being starved int.) submission. England stands in a position of what Mr.Goschen calls "splendid ieolation."And long may it be possible for us So keep free from the dangerous entanglements of foreign alliances. But in case of war, which Heaven forbid, a splendid Isolation may be converted into a far from splendid " deeolation."And therefore it becomes the duty of wise men to take every possible precaution against such a dread contingency. Until we get international disarma- ment, for which the world unfortunately is not yet ripe, It remains true that preparedness for war is a safeguard for reace. Now, it is well known that the strength of an army depends not only on the number and bravery of its soldiers, or the riflos which they carry, but also on the way in which they are fed. If the cemmissarist department breaks down, the best army in the world will be beaten. As the strength of a chain is no greater than that of its weakest link,so the strength of an attack or defence is at its weakest point. And I contend that the

div.head: VVIIAIC POINT OF ENGLAND'S DIIFSSCH
div.p: VVIIAIC POINT OF ENGLAND'S DIIFSSCH

In the contingencies aforesaid would be thil-i;CI that we could only feed about owe-fourth of the population out of our home resources. If this be so, then the depopu- lation of the country districts, the turning of millions of acres down into grass, and the consequently reduced power of feeding ouiselves, become dangers which we cannot afford to despise. None of our possible antagon- ists' are exposed to the same danger to anything like the same extent as we are. In time of war the ten thousand vessels which convey the raw material for our manufac- tories, and the hulk of our staple food-stuffs, would un- doubtedly have to run the gauntlet of hostile cruisers. Our very national existence might rest upon whether or not they could do that successfully. In any case, we should have to detach from the main line of defence a cnnsiderable force for their protection. And the ha Yoe which can be wrought upon peaceful traders by one active and dating war-ship was well shown by the depredations of the historic Alabama. For " the wolf does not care hew many the sheep are." "At the first shot fired in a general European war," sal I a leading American journal, "Eng- land should lay in a year'e supply of wheat, or rua the risk of being starved." Better that method than nothiog. But better still the brieging of our wheat-lands into cal- tivation, so that a large proportien, if not all, of the corn we need may be British grown. In the light of my argument this step beconaes a question of unusual and indeed vital importance. The land must be made access- ible to the cultivetors,or would-be cultivators ;the small farmer must have equal rights and facilities with the large farmers ; every tenant most have full property in his improvements, and in every possible way, save by the re-imposition of the old bad Corn-Laws, the growing 1 of corn should be encouraged and fostered. It would take time. Every reform takes that. Aud the best will never be made of the land so long as it is controlled by the one class which has starved Englishmen before now for the sake of its high rents, and is still guided by the same mistaken belief that the land was intended for its especial benefit before all others. A WHEAT CORNER.

And then there is another fact which must be taken into account. According to the latest transatlantic re- ports, Mr. Curzon's brother-in-law, one Leiter, of Chi- cargo,is aiming at the creation of a gigantic wheat nor- net. Already he has secured control of 12,000,000 huahels of wheat,or one-sixth of the yield of the United Kingdom. Whether or not he will be able to completely carry out his design to control Vie wheat markets of the world remains to be seen. He may burn his fingers over it as others have done. But his action at least points to the possibility of a few millionaires in America making enormous fortunes, " beyond the dreams of avarice," by charging famine prices in England's hour of need.Flndeed here is a danger even in times of peace, that rich monopolists should be able to corner the staple food for a great eation,and bring dire want into its cot- tage homes. And the only way It can he effectively pre- vented is by a juster land system. For there could be no monopoly of wheat without a monopoly of the land; and none need starve,no matter what the price of wheat, when they could get land sufficient to grow food thereon for their own consumption.

div.head: OREA.T SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL
div.p: OREA.T SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL

A meeting of this Council was held in the Board Schools prior to the annual meeting on Monday evening. Mr. T. Halton presided, and there were also present: Mr. W. Taylor, Mr. T. Cooke, Mr. T. Kilshow, Mr. G. Thompson, and Mr, J. Smith (clerk).

div.head: BRIDGE OVER THE SANKEY CANAL.
div.p: THE BRIDGE OVER THE SANKEY CANAL.

The Clerk read a copy of the letter he had forwarded to the Lancashire County Council calling attention to the unsuitability of the canal bridge at Sankey Bridges for highway purposes, and also to the enormous traffic pasaing over it,and he reported that he had received the following communication in reply :—" County Council Offices, Preston I have referred your letter of the 21st inst re turn bridge at Sankey Bridges to our District Surveyor for enquiry and report. but I may say at once that the County Council have at present no jurisdiction over canal or private bridges. They have.however,pro- moted a bill in the present session of Parliament called "The Lancashire County Council (Bridges) Bill under which they hope to obtain powers for the improvement of private bridges and for contributing to the widening I and improving of the railway and canal bridges. But such Bill will not receive the Queen's assent until about May next. In the meantime,instructions will be given to our district surveyor to keep the matter well in view. Yours etc., CanonloPll H. Sadler, Deputy Clerk to the County Council."—The Clerk informed the Council that at the suggestion of the Chairman he had written to the County Surveyor offering to meet him whenever he visited the district, but no reply had yet been received to this letter." PROPOSED IMPROVEMENT AT PENEETTE LANE END. The Chairman informed the members of the Council that Mr. Thompson and himself had met Mr. Selby as arranged at Peoketh-lane end on the previous Wednes- day. Mr. Selby expressed the opinion that it was a matter for the Highway Board and he (Mr. Halton) promised to bring it before that body. He did so at a meeting held a day or two afterwards, with the result that a deputation consisting of Captain Withington,J.P., Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., and himself (Mr. Halton) went in company with Mr. Thompson (the Highway Board's surveyor) to the spot. The deputation were agreed that an improvement should be made, and the surveyor was of opinion that a slight encroachment had been made. The Council might rest assured that the improvement would be carried forward by the Highway Board. This concluded the Council's busineqs,and an adjourn- ment was afterwards made to the large roam of the school where the annual parish meeting was held. A report of the proceedings will be found in another column.

Even in America the society idol occasionally takes to the stage, awl when that is the case, can count on a newspaper netoriety vita out of porportion to any talent he or she may possess. At the moment the New York papers are devoting pages of space to the daughter of a Californian millionaire in Madame Modjeska's corn- pany. Miss Northam, the young lady in question, de- clares that she has " vegetated in society and got such a sickening of it that her soul revolted," whence her desire for the stage. Among her obiter dicta are that " actors in grease paint and make-up are horrid things " who are " merely machines that make the play go round," with- out these accesswiee they are " simply stupid." As for " temptations," it is reassuring to be told that she has found far less in stage life than she encountered at her father's "pink teas, yellow, luncheons and crushed-straw berry dinners."

div.p: NOTES AD NEWS.

A striking testimony to the value of allotments is offered by the present Vicar of Granborough, Bucks, in the current " Spectator." Just a quarter of a centuiy ago the present Dean of Ely, then vicar of Granborough, let part of his glebe in half-scre lets to the labourers of the parish by way of expermen'. He was able to give a very satisfactory acoou it of the results when he wrote his well-known book" Land and the Labourers " a few years later. Ele let the land at sixty-six shillings an acre, a reit far in excess of the normal rent in the dis- drict, and found that the allotment holders were never- th-lea able to make eubitantisl profits. The present Vicar, Mr Newman, now states that the success of the experiment is beyond questi Since the time of Dean Stubbs the allotments have been multiplied. " More wheat is grown on the " allotments than in all the rest of the parish put together,and while all the clergy round are deplorin., the fall in rents the Vicars of Granborough have only had to roduc i their rents from guineas to pounds." Pauperism has declined ; no able-bodied man has for soma years had to fall upon the parish in ' the winter." The village labourers have established a flourishing co-operativs store, and are now trying to ap- ply co-operative principles to the production of eggs for ' the London market. In brief, this little Buckingham- , shire village is on the high road to prosperity, largely I through the wise policy of giving the 'hooters a direct interest in the land initiated by Dean Stubbs in 1873.

M may lending is an evil that, in the opinion of Some very experienced men, requires to be kept under very close surveillance. Sir George Lewis the other day sin- ge ted that judges should have p)wee to cut down the rate of interest,and Judge Collier,ln his evidence before the Mmey-lending Committee, put forward a scheme for the registration of small loans In the same way as bills of sale are registered. Now Mr. Justice Hawkins has been before the committee, and he, speaking with all the we'ght of his crest knowledge and experience, Proposes more drastic restrictions than either Sir George Lewis or Judge Collier. Mr. Justice Hawking would In many respects treat moneylenders in the same way as pawnbrokers. He thinks they should be registered, and that their licenses alien' I be subject to esdorsement for bad practises- He would, like Sir George Lewis, give Judges power to reduce the rate of interest, and would, moreover,make th, m come last among all creditors. The relegation of the moneylender's claim to the position of a "deferret" security would be a severe blow,espec,ally when linked with the limitation of the rate of interest.

The learned judge would alio give the police access to money-lender's books in the same way as to paws- brokers', and would not allow the same person to carry on business in different names in various towes. He seems, too, to be at direct variance with Judge Collier as to money-lending companies. These,in Judge Collier's opinion, do on the whole a legitimate and conscionable business, but Mr. Justice Hawkins would not allow money-'enders to trade as limited companies at all. If, however, he is severe upon companies, he would be equally trenchant in dealing with money-lenders who describe themselves as " private gentlemen." These people he weuld consign to prison forthwith. He is, in fact,in favour of compelling all money-lenders to appear under their true colours,and of framing the law so as to keep them from plundering the unfortunate people who deal with them. The evils to be cured are fraud on the pert of the money-lender and betting and gamb- ling on the part of the borrowers ; but while Judge Collier would proceed by exposing the borrower, Mr. Justice Hawkins deals with the lender alone.

How true it is that it is better to invent a sauce or a safety-pin as a means to wealth than to discover a gold. mine. The personalty of the late Mr. C. Wheeby Lea, of Lea and Perrin' s sauce fame, has been sworn at £1,070,000, and the realty at £29,000. The estate duty already paid exceeds £BB,OOO, buli that amount will be swelled by a sum of £25,000 in legacy duties, which the estate has to bear. The deceased made bequests of £lOO,OOO each to two nephews and a !seine in South Australia. One nephew is dead, and his widow gets in- stead t 5,000. Mrs. Lea—the widow—gets £50,000 and the real estate. Beyond these items there are some sixty 'bequests te distant relatives, thirty to servants, and others to Worcester 'charitable institutiens, the total amount thus disposed ol amounting to £350,000. The 'widow is the residuary legatee, and will receive in all / about half a million.

The deceased's late partner left a fortune of nearly equal amount—amassed, like Mr. Lea's, wholly from the &mous sauce. The recipe of this was given to them when they were chemists in a modest way of business at Broad-street, Worcester, by the late Lord Sandys,who had picked it up casually in Ins Indian travels. The firm kept it by them for years without suspecting the wealth it embodied. Lord Sandys called at the shop when all the world was beginning to talk of the appetis- ing sauce and humorously suggested that he would like to share in the proceeds. The late Mr. Perrin replied complacently that Lord Sandra might share in the pro- fits if he would stand behind the counter and assist in the sale.

Mr. Chaplin on Tuesday brought a Bill into the HOllBB of Commons to amend the law with respect to vaccina- tion, and stated that the Royal Comrnision recommended that lymph should be placed within the reach •f all, and that no parents should be required to submit their chil- dren for vaccirmtion by means of anything but calf lymph. Both these recommendations had been accepted While the bill provided that vaccination would continue to be obligatory, vaccination by anything hut calf lymph would cease to be compulsory. Vaccination from arm. to arm would cease to be compulsory with lymph supplied from other sources than glycerine lymph, end In future the doctor would go to the child's house instead of the child going to the vaccination station. The period within which a child must be vaccinated would also kw exten- ded to twelve months. Where a person conscientousil objected to vaccination he would be liable to two prose- cutions under two sections of the existing Act, but the liability to repeated penalties would be abolished. The bill was read a first time.

Commenting on the common causes of nervous disor. ders,Prof. W. H. Thompson says :—The message of mo- dern science about the nervous system is more hopeful than ever. It tells us th at the nervous system has a greater store of reserve vitality than all the other bodily systems put together. It is the only texture that is found not to have lost weight after death by starvation, as well as after death by any cause. It is the last to grow old, As to the mindit need not grow old at all, provided it be steadilv applied with that mighty spiri- tual element in us which we call interest. Even the muscular system can la,s wonderfully sustained by inter est ; for should a man attempt the same muscular work ,n a treadmill which he lightly endures along tbe moun- tain brook after a trout,he w-uld faint dead away. But the mind will by interest grow steadily, even while bone and sinew are wasting through as.

WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Registrar Ridgway. Re TRomas Moonzs.—This debtor appeared for o further examination in bankruptcy. At the first hearing of the case it was stated that the liabilities of the debtor who carried on business as a grocer at 21, Irlam-street, Warrington, amounted to £lB3B 12s. 7d., but four creditors were fully secured for .£1,198 6s. 7d. leaving the liabilities to rank at .£638 19s. 9d. The assets were estimated to pro- duce .£351 16s. Bd., leaving a deficiency of £287 3s. ld.—Mr. Longton appeared on behalf of the debtor.—The Assistant Official Receiver(Mr.Potter) stated that he had just asked the debtor whether he had found anybody who was willing to make an , offer for the equity of the dwelling-house and shop ; as instructed at the last Court. but he was surprised ,1 to hear from the debtor that he did not understand that he was to seek a customer.—The Debtor: I can only say that I thought the matter was taken out of my hands entirely.—The Assistant Official Re.l eiver: This is a sample of the help the debtor gives s.—Mr. Longton : It has been a clear roisunder- blending on the debtor's part and mine. lam sure asr. Moores would have been willing to give any sdsistance he could.—The Assistant Official Re- ceiver: At the last Court the debtor said the equities would be worth £l4s.—The Debtor: I have had several enquiries with respect to the matter, but have told the parties to com- municate with the Official Receiver.—The Assist- ant Official Receiver: I want you to understand that no one has made any offer at all approaching to .£145. I shall be glad to know of anyone who will give anything like it.—Mr. Longton : It would be nonsense for anyone to give that amount,. I know a party that will make an offer.—The Assist- ant Official Receiver said be had no further ques- tions to ask, and the Registrar asked the Creditors present if they wished to cross-examine the debtor. —Mr. William Scotson : Are your children possessed of any property 2—No.—You have not transferred any property to them 2—No.—lf your children say they are provided for they are saying what is not true then ?—Yes—Do you know that they have said so don't know what they say, but if they say so it is not correct.—Have you given any guarantee to the Globe Company 2 No.—Wbat was the amount of your mother's estate at the time of her death?—A little over £2,000.1 cannot exactly tell the amount.—Who were the executors 7—My brother Abel and myself.—Wasn't Abel dead before your mother died?—Yes he was dead, and I was the only executor. The events were so near togetber that I forgot at the time.—What did the estate consist of 2—House property chiefly—Wasn't your mother insured for £l,ooo?—Yes; the estate would amount to about .£3,ooo.—What was your share:of that sum?—l think it was between £3OO and £4OO.— Is it not a fact that there was only one brother alive at the time in addition to yourself P—l am not quite sure. I know that a brother in America received. his share.—How much did he receive—About MOO —Where did the remainder of the estate go to7—lt was equally divided I know, and I think it was about .£3OO apiece.—The Assistant Official Re- ceiver : May I suggest that it would better to adjourn the examination to the 15th of April, in order that the debtor may file an account showing to disposition of the residual estate of his father and mother, and produce the vouchers—Mr. Long- ton I think the creditors are pursuing a shadow in insisting upon it—The Registrar : They are en- titled to this information—The Assistant Official Receiver (to debtor) : Have you got the accounts relating to the disposal of this estate, or have your !olicitors ?—The Debtor : I expect they will be included in the papers I gave you—The Registrar adjourned the further examination of the debtor until the 15th of April,instructing the debtor to see his solicitors for the' accounts of the estate, and if they had not got them to go over to Manchester and find them at the Official Receiver's office, early next week.

THE APPROACHES TO PADGATE BRIDGE. The Surveyor reported that Mr. Thornton and himself inspected the :approaches with res- pect to this Brides. Mr. Scott, the engineer to the Cheshire Lines C-Aninittee was agree- able to the improvements proposed, and which were leo forth on the accompanying plan. The railway company would give the Board the small strip of land required for widening the approaches.—Mr. Thornton said it was in accordance with something before the Board a short time ago.—Mr. William Houghton thought it was a pity to interfere with the road at the bott-in of the bridge. It had only just recently been made and a now fence erected, and it would require a great dr al of material CO fill up the place where it was intended to widen the road. Be considered it a very fantaatic improvement, and be thought the Board ought to deal with more urgent work. —Mr. Thornton said it was a matter of great import,. ance, and the parishioners pressed the matter forward. Be moved that the Board approve of the proposed improvement, and that the Surveyor be instructed to ascertain the cost of the land required :at one side of the bridge.—The Chairman seconded the pioposition.—Mr. Houghton moved that the improvement be not approved.—Mr. J. At present the Surveyor had nowhere to put the dirt fronl the roads,and it could be tipped there without difficulty. —Mr. James Houghton said he hoped Mr. Thornton did not refer to him as -opposing every improvement for Padgate.—Mr,Thornton : Yes,to be straight,l did.—Mr. William Houghton said he would be willing to withdraw the amendment if a committee were appointed te inspect the place, and report to the next meeting. div.head: ASSESSMENT OF PUBLICHOUSES IN WA.IOINGTON.
div.p: THE ASSESSMENT OF PUBLIC- HOUSES IN WA.IOINGTON.

A QUESTION FOR THE RATEPAYERS. With the near approach of the election of the Board of Guardians it is advisable that the rate- payers should be placed in possession of a few facts relating to this subject. Primarily it is a matter to be dealt with by the Assessment Committee, but that authority is,of course, appointed by the Board of Guardians. We have published articles dealing with the assessment of public-houses on several oc- casions during the past three years and yet nothing has been done by the committee to re-assess the licensed houses in the town,some of which are ad- mittedly at a very low figure. The inactivity of the Warrington Assessment Committee on this sub- ' ject is in striking contrast with the decisive action which has been taken, and is still n progress, in many of the neighbouring towns At Accrington, , for instance, a re-assessment of the licensed houses has just been made, and their assessment which previously stood at £4,075, will for the next three years be rated at £5,840, making a difference of £1,765 in the rateable value. The net result in this case to the ratepayers generally is that the drink interest will have to contributesoo a year more to the borough funds—equal to a saving of a penny in the pound on the rates. The North Manchester overseers are following the example of Accrington, and a re-assessment of the public-houses in the Union is in progress. Other Union assessors are also on the same track, but not so in Warrington. _ _ _

There has been no re-assessment of licensed houses in Warrington since 1894, There were then in the town 87 fully licensed houses, 45 beernouses, and 74 off licences, and the net increase made in the assessments of these places was almost £1,500. Nil, increase has been made since that date, and yet the town has increased at a faster rate in the years that have since elapsed than at any previou time in its history. This has beneficially affecte the owners of the licensed houses who are not placed at the same disadvantage as other tradesmen in having increased competition. In fact the num- ber of drink shops has slightly diminished in the centre of the town, thus making those that remain still more valuable.

_ In a town like Warrington where most of the licensed houses are "tied houses " there is a great difficulty in arriving at the true assessment of a licensed house. It is a well-known tact that the rent charged to a tenant is sometimes of a nominal character, and not by any means commensurate with the value of the house. This point can be best illustrated' by one or two typical instances. A few years ago the Warrington Corporation became the owners ot two licensed houses,the Baths Hotel and the Queen's Hotel, both of Which are situated in Sankey-street. At the time of purchase the Baths Hotel was owned by the Bedford Brewery Company and the assessment in 1893—before the purchase by the Corporation—was £47 10s. gross and .£4O 10s. rateable. The Corpora- tion offered the Hotel to the tenant who was pre- pared to give the highest rental, and on the rental obtained the Assessment Committee were able to Increase the assessment to £l4O gross and £ll9 Irateable, or about three times as much as the pre- vious assessment ! With reference to the Queen's Hotel, that was in the possession of Mr. Lawrence Flood at the time of purchase and the assessment Was £7O gross and ..£59 10s. rateable. When the Corporation came into possession, and obtained a tenant at a competition rental the assessment was raised to £l3O gross and £llO 10s. rateable; or al- most double the previous assessment. It will therefore be seen that where the Assess- ment Committee are able to ascertain the true rental of a licensed house, the assessraent is at once very largely increased. But what is to be said of houses still 'tied" to the brewers ? Let us take the Talbot Hotel in Sankey-street, for example, which seems to occupy as good a position for busi- ness as either the Queen's Hotel or the Baths Hotel. The assessable value of that hotel is £7O gross and .E 59 10s. rateable or just the same as the Queen's Hotel before the Corporation became the owners. Many other instances could be given—in fact a number have already appeared in this paper in a series of interviews with a local manufacturer who has taken a deep interest in the subject. We will, however, give our readers a a few to consider for themselves. The value of the Feathers Hotel in Bridge-st. in the estimation of the owner is .£16,000, and yet the Assessment Com- mittee think £75 gross and .£64 rateable an equit- able assessment! Taking the whole of the public- houses in the town it will be found that very few are assessed at the same figures as the two hotels owned by the Corporation. This will be seen when it is stated that the following are the assessments of a number of well-known houses in the town: Pelican hotel, ..CBO gross, .£6B rateable; Royal Couit hotel, .£9O gross, £76 rateable; Eagle and Child, .£76 108. gross, .£65 rateable; Coffee House, Horse- market-st., .£9O gross, £76 10s. rateable; crown and Sceptre, £BO gross, £6B rateable; Cross Keys, .£6O gross, .£5l rateable; Waggon and Horses £6O gross, .£5l rateable; Raven hotel, ..£BO gross, £6B rateable; Moulders Arms, Mersey-st., £55 gross, £47 rateable. It is to be hoped that tile candidates who are now seeking re-election on the Board of Guardians will Ibe urged to ask for a re-assessment of the public- houses of the town on again entering office.
