superior to the attack. This feature is a characteristic of the West Lancashire clubs just now. They have very little brilliancy of method or scoring power, but as tacklers and defenders they will take a lot of licking. Bate and Duckworth were the best couple on the home side. All the three quarters did good work at times but it was individual and not combined. Raynor seemed to nervous to de anything in the second half. For the win- ners, Butterworth, Jolley, and Faulkner played a grand game, the two former being perfect. The sturdy little centre seems better than ever and is the backbone of the Runcorn team. Jolley's display was far in front of Boa- cow's and could not have been beaten even by Sam Houghton. Woods was the weak spot and was very much on a par with Raynor for mulling the ball. The forwards were about equal, Deakin, Naylor and Mason shining for vVarrington, and Farmer,Walker and Bettley showing up well for Runcorn. By the way this is the last of Warrington's league matches at Wilderspool, and there is scarcely any possibility of any more points being obtained in the league. Runcorn have passed Warring- ton in the table.and there is some probability of Wigan, Leigh and St. Helens doing likewise.

Warrington are undoubtedly on the down-grade this season. Their display is poorer each succeeding Satur- day, snd without Smack Bate would be hardly equal to that of a second class team. There will undoubtedly have to be a weeding out for next season. Some really fast, clever men, are sorely needed, and I hardly think the rather conservative cammittee will be able to resist the growing feeling in favour of outside help. Such men as Bate and Barber are really wasted in a team composed as Warrington is.

A fixture with Manningham has been arranged for to-day, the venue being on the Yorkshire club's ground. There has been another process of juggling with the players to raise a team. Now we find the committee in their dire extremity, place Duckworth in the centre, with young Bate helping his brother behind the pack. Hallam goes wing once more. It may be an improve- ment,but that the arrangement will be a Success against Manningham is too much to expect.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

RUGBY FOOTBALL. watery has again repeated itself in the shape of another triumph over Warrington by Runcorn. Since the formation of thl Northern union the two clubs have burieditheir differences with the hatchet, and their meet- ings in League encounters are fraught with the same keenness and enthusiasm as of yore. A fast and exciting game is a certain result, and the issue is , a matter of doubt to the close, though the Cestrians have, for years, just pulled it off and know not what defeat is at the hands of Warrington. The match at Runcorn in the early part of the Beason wag won by the homesters— rather lockily,—a goat and a try, to a try being the score. Since then both of them have had some hard knocks, but the Cestrians seem to be recovering again, as their neighbours deterioriate,and notwithstanding the fact that Warrington entered the arena with a full deter- mination to avenge themselves, they had once more to defeat on their own ground.

There was an unexpectedly large crowd to witness the battle. as gates have dwindled somewhat in War- rington of late, but interest in this old-time fixture is apparently still maintained. The Runcornians, either from a low estimate of Warrington's abilities or from a high estimate of Oldham's power—l prefer the latter reason—arrived at Warrington minus three of their bast men. If anything this should have increased the con- fidence of the homesters and made their prospect a brighter one. Probably it did,but the prospect lost some of its pristine brightness before the close of play. A couple of points which will be warmly appreciated on the other side of the Mersey, were taken away by the boys in green.

The game throughout was a most interesting exhibi tion,and though the tactics of neither side approached e- very high class there was a dash FIGI vigour about the play which rendered it fascinating. In weight and speed the two teams were excellently well balanced, and a close game was a very easy preenction before the _ commencement of the match. Up to half time Warring_ ton had rather the best of matters and troubled the " Lineetts "more than a trifle. For about ten minutes a most persistent attack on the Runcorn line was main- tained,and Bate, Moores,and Rayner,all came very near scoring. The defence was splendid at every point bow- ever,and before long the home line had been subjected to a close but equally unproductive siege. When the whistle proclaimed the interval,neither side bad scored. and each had had an equal amount of attack and de- fence.

There was every reason to believe that Warrington would pull it off in the concluding portion, but fate willed otherwise. In a style which we have got used to of late the play of the home team deteriorated consider- ably as the struggle progressed. The backs were slower and fielded the ball slovenly, Raynor being a particu- larly bad offender in this respect. Combination—scarce before—now became absolutely non est and Runcorn Showed a corresponding improvement all round. The play of Jolley and Butterworth in particular was magni. &eat. Not a kick from Warrington but was returned with interest, while one or two pretty sequences of pass- ing went very near to penetrating the home defence. Tine wore on, and it seemed all over bar shouting with nothing scored, when the irrepressible Betterworth to)k a pass in front of the pests and just tipped the oval over. So near was it to a miss that a goodly proportion of the crowd would even yet stake their inheritance on the assertion that it was "no goal." I give Butterworth the credit of it however. It certainly settled the matter. Warrington had only just time to dash the tears from their eyes and make a fruitless sally before the final whistle was heard proelaiming Runcorn's victory. 1 e h i o h been ver ha: „er e. I don't really think either side deserved to win. They c-ere so evenly matched that a draw ly wul d *he fairest result. With the leaders engaged in a mere "friendly"fixture, chief interest in the Lancashae Senior Competition centred in the meeting of Swinton and Widnes. Either the" dark blues " have returned to their best form, or the " Chemicals" were in one of their utterly unreliable moods,as the game ended in a ridiculously easy win for Swinton,wbo should now have no difficulty in finishing second.and might indeed jest reach first place in case Oldham were to meet with an " accident" or two. The remaining engagements were not of paramount impor- tance. A lively game at St. Helens ended in a draw of 14 points each between them and Salforo,whilst Brough- ton Ranzera satisfactorily accounted for Leigh. The I only other engagement was the one at Stockport, where Rochdale Hornets were beaten, and consigned definitely ' to the last two in the table, Morecame, of course, being certainties for the " wooden spoon."
The third round in the Northern Union Cup ties will be played to-lay (Saturday). The matches will be played on the ground of the first 13w-fled club and are as follow :

div.head: BILLIARDS IT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
div.p: BILLIARDS IT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

An exhibition match was played at the Conserva- tive Club on Wednesday night between Mr. H. J. Longton and Mr. James Carnm before a large com- pany. The game was 500 up and both players started on level terms and in the result Mr. Camm was returned the victor by 115 points. The winner's highest break was 39 and his opponents 24.

div.head: FIRE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: FIRE AT EARLESTOWN.

On Thursday evening an alarm was given that a fire had broken out on the premises of Mrs. King, confectioner, Earlestown. Pedestrians in Bridge- street about 8 o'clock observed flames in an upper room, and an inspection showed that the window draperies were burning in an alarming manner, the inflammable material having come in contact with the gas. Prompt measures were taken and before anything of a very serious nature took place the curtains and blinds were destroyed. CHILD SCALDED LT EARLESTOWN.

On Sat-t;Cli; rafternoon a child about 3 years of age son of George Rhubottom and grandson of Mr. Martin, chip potato dealer,Grant-street, Earlestown was dangerously scalded by falling into a pan of boiling fat. The child was visiting at Martin's, and in the room where it was playing were two or three pans of the boiling fat. It stood near one of them, and thinking it saw a mouse, stepped back and sat in one of the pans. The child was rescued immediately by Mr. Martin, who applied the usual remedies and sent for • Dr. Mounsey, who found the little fellow to be very seriously injured and his condition has since continued serious. CATHOLIC BALL AT EARLESTOWN.

At the Town Hall, Earlestown on Wednesday night, St. Patrick's anniversary was celebrated by a soiree given under the auspices of the Michael Devitt branch of the Irish National League. The hall was very prettily decorated, the Irish National colours being prominent. There were 85 couples present, and dancing which commenced at 8-30,was continued.with unabated enbrgy until after five o'clock next morniug. Messrs. Appleton's string band furnished the music, and the dancers were under the care of Messrs. Turton, Flernirg and T. Burke, who acted as M.C.'s. The catering for the refreshment of the inner man was in the capable hands of Mr. W. Beatty. The soiree was a great success. The Irish Distress fund to which the proceeds were devoted, will be agreeably aug- mented.

THE HOMES FOR WAIFS AND STAYS. At the Wargrave Church on Sunday, special ser- mons were preached by the Rev. E. It. Tarbuck, secretary to the society for providing homes for waifs and strays. Thera were fair congregations, especially at the evening service,when the preacher dwelt at sozn longth upon the work and objects of the society, which he said were the reclamation of gutter children,and others,who for their better con- dition have to be removed out of the keeping of cruel and drunken parents. Ills observations bore chiefly upon the work in the East end of London, where he had laboured for some years. He pointed out that the society was maintained solely by vol- untary effort, and wade an urgent appeal for sub- scriptions. Collections were made at each service in aid of the Society.

DxAThOF Mn. A. PURNELL. This week we have to record the death of Mr. Arthur Purnell, which took place at his late resi- dence in Wargrave-road, on Saturday afternoon last, after an illness extending over six weeks, at the age of 44 years. The deceased gentleman who had been engaged some 12 or 13 years as cashier and traveller for the firm of Messrs. John Slee and Co., engineers, Earlestown, was seized about two months ago with an attack of erysipelas, from which he recovered. About a fortnight afterwards, a relapse ensued, and despite the ability and attention of Dr. Handyside, he never recovered, and expired as stated above. He leaves a widow and one son. The interment took Place on Wednesday afternoon at Wargr!tve Chnrch. The body was followed to its last resting place by Arthur Purnell, son; Mr. John Slee (brother-in-law), Master John Slee (nephew), Mr. Joseph Shillcock (Warrington), Mr. A. Bridgewater (cousin), Mr. W. Attfteld, Mr. C. Bateman, Mr. R. Molyneux, Sweet- love, Mr. L. Cutts, and about 30 of the employes of Messrs. Slee and Co. The bearers were Messrs. J. W. Hipwood. J. Shepherd and R. Jones. The service was conducted by the Rev. J. Carson. A large number of floral tributes were placed upon the coffin, and in addition to those sent by the relatives, there were others sent'lw Mr.and Mrs.Borron,Messrs Starkte, Sweetlove,Brierley and Siddeloy,and a very handsome anchor subscribed by the employes at the works.

PERSONAL. Thß condition of Mr. J. Killsley, instructor of the Warriugton Gymnasium, who is lying ill at his residence in Leigh-street,this week shows consider- able improvement. Mr. William Long, and Councillor Bennett at- tended the 38th annual meeting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce (which was held in Lon- don this week) as the delegates of the Warrington Chamber.

_ WARD/NGTON COUNTY COITD.T. ABitting of this court was held on Thursday be- fore his 14.onour Judge Wynne Pfoulkes. The busi- ness transacted included 217 original plaints, nine adjourned plaints, seven default summonses, 92 judgment summonses, and one application for an administration order. There was no business of public interest. The removal of the offices to Pal- myra Square has now been completed, and on Mon- day the business will be conducted there. The further hearing of the claim for wrongful dismissal against the ;Cheshire Lines Committee was ad- journed until the 31st inst., when it will be beard at the new County Court. HAYDOCK AND WADDINGTON COUNTY COURT. Mr. J. W. Green, solicitor, of St. Helens, on Wed- nesday had the satisfaction of receiving a letter from Sir Charles Lennox Peel, clerk of the Privy Council, intimating that the Order transferring Hasdock from Warrington to the St.flelens County Court district had been passed, and will on the let July next come into force. Mr.Oreen initiated the movement so far back as September, 1893, and has all through acted on behalf of the tradespeople of Haydock,to whom the change will be of great con- venience and result in a saving of time and money. In answer to a memorial from the Ilaydock trades- men, the then Local Board memorialized the Leri Chancellor on the matter. The memorial was pre- sented in March, 1894, by the Hon. T.Nir.Legh.tnem- her for the Newton Division. who. along with the Right Hon. Viecount Cross. Lord Privy Seal, has rendered valuable assistance in the matter. Linder the Ord,r passed by her Majesty in Council on the 7th inst Ilaydock now forms part of the St. Helens diArict.

div.head: EARLESTOWN SOCIAL CYCLING CLUB.
div.p: EARLESTOWN SOCIAL CYCLING CLUB.
PHESRNTATION TO THE SECRETARY.

Tho second annual dinner and smoking concert in connection with the above club, took place under 6 u.:,- cessful conditions at the headquarters, Wellington Hotel, Eirist,wn on Tuesday evening. There was a good C ,cipPmy assembled round the festive board, and full justice was done to the good things provided. After the remov.l of the cloth, the subsequent proceedings were presided over by Mr. C. Chorlton, the vice-chair being occupied by Councillor P. Machtiahon. Amingst those present were Councillor Gilmour, Dr. Patterson, Mr. T. W. Thorpe,

r The Cnairman said be was extremely obliged for the h mour the committee had done him at their second annual dinner and smoking concert. The councillors present would be extremely obliged if no questions were asked them respecting the loudness of the township. Ha thought such remarks would bn out of place as they got quite enough badgering at the Town Hall (Hear, hear.) There was much to be said in favour of cycling, and he thought there was very little to say against it. He was not a practical cyclist himself although he was a member of that club. The only thing he could son against cycling was riders going distances when they had a holiday, and were not in training; it was, he thought, injurious to the system, and another evil was the low handles. When the bicycle was ri iden in a proper manner and the Isandles taken hold of in a right war, he had been told it helped to develope the muscles. Cycling helped to cultivate the mind by taking them through the country and displaying new scenes; it also helvd to deyelope courting and flirting, not only by the single, but by the married people. (Laughter.) He concluded by proposing " The Queen." An instrumental selection was g: v'm by Messrs. Apple. ton, Walsh,Huddleston, and Andertuo.

The Chairman proposed " The SJCItil C7cling Club" which he said was now in a prosperous condition, its membership having increa.erl 50 per cent since last year, many having joined skied thc Cycla parade. (Hear, hear).

Mr. W. H. Kay sang in excellent style " Anchored." Mr. T. Bowes responded on behalf of the club,remark- ing that it was three years since the club was originate,d and he thought the coming season would be a successful one. They were not great riders but they were sociable. (gear, hear). Mr. W. Sutton recited " The dying soldier," after which Councillor MacMahon proposed the health of "The Visitors." Sergeant Ritchie responded,and thanked them for the kind manner in which they had proposed the health of the visitors and for the handsome and cordial manner in which it had beEn re:ieived. On be- half of his colleagues ef the "C" troop of the Lancashire Hussars he thanked the committee for the kind manner in which they had entertained them. What they had done in connection with the cycle parade was not much, and if their services were ever required again, he had no doubt they could get permission from the Hon. T. W. Legh, to give them. (Applause.) Mr. W. Sephton sang " The Monarch of the Woods." Mr. C. H. Lea sang " The Young Brigade," Mr. J. Huddleston gave" Hooligan's Mule," and Mr. S. Swann sang" The Old Brigade." Mr. J. W. Thorpe afterwards addressing the secretary Mr. T. Waring, said the members of the club were so ' pleased with the way in which he had done his duties that they could not allow a time like that to naas ever without recognising It, and that being the annual meet- ing, they thought it was the t .ist time for the purpose. Mr. Bowes had told him that a presentation was taken UP so spontaneously sad heartily that if they had not stopped the subscriptions, they did not know to what extent it would have gone. Hs thou formally presented Mr. Waring with a handsome black ebony walking stick with ivory handle and silver mounts, and meerschaum pipe and case,and expressed the hope that he would live long to enjoy them both. (Applause.) The inscription on the stick was :—" Presented to Mr. Thomas Waring, by the members of the Earlestewn Social Cycline Club, in recognition of his services. March 15th, 1898."
Dr. Patterson propmed the health of The Secretary." Since the club was formed Mr. Waring had taken very great interest in it.

A man who took office with a fret, will ought not to expect anything when he did it as a hobbyeand that was a hobby of his. He had done what he could to make the club a succeqs, and:if there was anything he could do more he would do it. Ho thanked the donors for the gifts he had received. (Applause.) Mr. William O'Brien addressed an Irish meeting on Tuesday night at Hanley. He said the Irish National Party did not wish to be unjust to the Liberal party ; they were as strongly as ever for conciliation, but it must be on Mr. Gladstone's terms, without the subtrac- tion of a single clause. Home Rule would have to be the first business of any possible Home Rule Ministry. This was the only honourable position for members of the Liberal party to take up, and, as recent elections showed, the only safe position.

div.head: POPULAR LECTURES AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: POPULAR LECTURES AT EARLESTOWN.
THE EVOLUTION OF SCENERY.

The last of the series of lectures promoted' by the Newtonin-Makerfield Lecture Committee was delivered on Thursday evening in the Town Hall, Earlestovrn, before a large audience,by Dr.R.D.R.,berts, M.A.,F.G.5., his subject being "The evolution of Scenery • a study in Ga.:logy." In the absence of Mr. F. J. Woo, from ill- items, Mr. C. B. F. Barron presided. The Claairrnan said :that Mr. Wood was prevented from attending by illness, and he was taking that duty upon himself. He (the chairman) had the honour of occupying the chair at the first lecture of the series when Sir Robert Ball interested them with his lecture. He took them into other worlds and allowed their imagination to play with heavenly bodies. Dr. Roberts was going to remain on the earth and he (Mr. Borron) had no doubt he would instruct them just as much as Sir Robert Ball did. (Applause.) Dr. Roberts, in beginming his lecture, said that he had designedly introduced the word evolution into the title of his lecture because the main impression which was left upon the mind by the study of the different types of scenery and their origin,was that of evolution—develop- n:ent. Be then proceeded to ['ketch the larger features of the earth's surface, and to describe the structure of the great continental masses. For an explanation of these larger features the geologist turned to the science of astronomy for help. Astronomers taught that the earth was a great ball flattened at the poles rotating on its a xis and revolving round the sun. There were strong reasuee for chinking that it had been originally in a molten condition, and the evidence for this was mdi- cated by the lecturer, who showed that the interior of the earth was still in a highly heated cendition. He then sketched the conditions of things in the case of a cooling rotating MISS such as the earth had been, and compared the physical features of the earth with those that such a body might be expected to show. The distribution of land and water was referred to, the land areas having great mountain chains of contorted crumpled rock,torm- iag as it were their baekbones.Dr.Roberts then described the character of the two main groups of rocks composing the crust of the earth, the igeneous and the aqueous and their mode of formation. He men- tioned that the bulk of the rocks belonged to the aqueous group. He pointed out that the original surface rock must have belonged to the igneous group, although at the present time the bulk of the rocks were of the aqueous or sedimentary kind. He then proceeded to consider how it came about that whila the original rocks were igneous the bulk of the existing rocks were aqueows. l'his led to a discussion of the destruction of the land, i.e., the disintegration of rook masses under the action of tho sea, rain, frost and rivers. The lecturer suggested that the earth mieht he compared to a living thing. The characteristic of life was unceasing change, constant waste and renewal. He then, with a series of beautiful lantern slides thrown upon the screen, illustrated the processes of destruction which were constantly taking place. He showed by photographs of the rocky coastline in different parts of the country how the character of the scenery was dependent upon the difference in the nature and arrangements of the rocks and the character of the agencies acting upon them. The characteristic scenery est mountain regions and the forms of different kinds of valleys were similarly ex- plained and illustrated by means of photographic slides. The deposit formed as the resplt of this action had, by movements of upheaval, in due course, been elevated to form new land. The movements of upheaval were one of the manifestations of the action of internal forces —the igneous forces—which ale o manifested themselves in the phenomena of volcanic action, The lecturer then proceeded to show how additions to the land were made through the instrumentality of these igneous forces by the expulsion from the interior, during vulcanic eruptions of volcanic dust and ashes as well as the outpouring of melted rock in the, form of lava. He dealt with the products of volcanic eruplons in past geological time.; and finally treat(' i of the stupendous outburst of volcanic activity in Scotland and Ireland in the tertiary period, taking as a special illustration the remarkable structure of the Island of Egg, off the West coast of Scotland, where evidence is furnished on an impressive scale alike of the constructive internal forces and the destructive external forces. The Scuir of Eigg,a long mountain ridge twelve hundred feet above sea level, being really the remains of a lava flow that occu- pied a valley of tertiary times. Dr. Roberts concluded by pointing out that the earth's surface with its diverse science features was but the last link in a long chain of events, the beginning of which was lost in the mists of antiquity. (Applause). A vote of thanks to the lecturer at the close was moved by Dr. Handyside and seconded by Mr. Coiling. wood and heartily accorded, a similar compliment being paid the chairman. The Chairman, in response, said he thought it was due from him to ask them to pass a vote of thanks to the secretary, Mr. Ormand, who had done such a large amount of work in connection with the lectures. (Ap- plause.) He was sorry Mr. Ormand was unable to be Present, but in his name he would thank them fer the kind expression they had given to his suggestion.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS AND RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTIONS.
TIIE NOMINATIONS.

Twelve o'clock noon on Thursday was the last hour fixed on which nominations could be received for the election of Guardians of the Poor and Rural District Councillors. Mr. J.C. Sutton is the return- ing officer for the election of Guardians, and Mr. S. Sutton for the Rural District Councillors. It will be eeen from the appended nominations that unless a ;umber of candidates withdraw before 12 o'clock noon on Monday next, elections will take place in several wards and districts. In the Warrington Borough ten representatives aroreturned on the Board, and of these only five are at present unop- posed. These are Mrs. Clay, Mr. William Hickman, Mr. Alfred J. Jolley, Mr. T. B. Malkin, and Mr. S. Davies. The wards in which elections are prob- able are Fairfield ward where the candidates are Mr. Pilling and Dr. McCarthy; St. John's, where the Rev. W. H. Drummond and Mr. Battersby contest the seat ; St. Austin's (Sankey Bridges district), Mr. G. Thompson being °nosed by Mr. T. H. Ash- croft; Orford ward, where the retiring canclidtte— Mr. W. J. Shaw—will be opposed by Mrs.Edelsten ; and in Latchford ward, Mr. A. Jolley and Mr. W. J. Shaw are the two candidates nominated. With respect to the other parts of the Union, it may be stated that in the district of Newton-le-Willows there will be no contests whatever for the four vacant seats. A vacancy occurs in one of the three wards into which Haydock is divided, owing to the resignation of the Rev. Father Moore. The two other retiring guardians—the Rev. J. H. Rid- dette and Mr. J. Billinge—have been returned unopposed. Coming to the smaller districts for which the guardian is also the rural councillor there is a prospect of several interesting contests. In Penketh, Mr. J. Dignum, the retiring member will be opposed by Mr. R. B. Matthews, whilst in Poulton-with-li'eartthead there are three candidates in the field viz: Mr. William Bennett, Mr. Henry Thornton, and Mr. George Slather. The retiring Guardian was Mr. John, Houghton who ' does not seek re-election. There will also be con- tests in Rixton-with-Glazebrook, and Burtonwood. There may, of course, be several withdrawals before noon on Monday, and in that case the position of I affairs will be altered.
